# Buying groups: why your champion is outnumbered and how to sell to consensus

> Forrester puts the typical B2B purchase at 13 internal stakeholders and nine external influencers, and Gartner found 74% of buying teams show unhealthy conflict. A champion cannot carry that alone. Sell to consensus: get the group to agree on the problem and its cost, give the champion a one-page case to forward, and ask who else must agree.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/buying-group-consensus/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- A typical B2B purchase now involves 13 internal stakeholders and nine external influencers, according to Forrester's 2026 research.
- Gartner found that 74% of B2B buying teams show unhealthy conflict, and groups that reach consensus are 2.5 times more likely to report a high-quality deal.
- Content tailored to individuals can hurt consensus; Gartner measured a 59% negative impact, while buying-group relevance improved consensus by 20%.
- The seller's job shifts from winning the champion to helping the group agree on the problem and what it costs.
- Ask one question on every call: who else needs to agree with this?

Most sales methods still center on the [champion](/glossary/#champion): the person inside the buyer who wants the change. The champion matters. But the champion is now one voice in a crowded room, and most of that room never meets the seller. This guide gives the current numbers on [buying groups](/glossary/#buying-group), explains why consensus predicts deal quality, and sets out a practical kit for selling to the whole group.

## How big is a B2B buying group in 2026?

A typical B2B buying group has about ten or more people, and recent research puts it higher once outside advisers are counted. The main public sources:

| Source | Finding |
|---|---|
| Forrester, State of Business Buying 2026 | 13 internal stakeholders and nine external influencers in a typical buying decision |
| Forrester, State of Business Buying 2024 | 13 people involved on average; 89% of purchases span two or more departments |
| 6sense, Buyer Experience Report 2025 | Buyers evaluated about five vendors on average; 79% initiated first contact; nearly 4,000 buyers surveyed |
| Gartner, buyer survey published May 2025 | 74% of buying teams showed unhealthy conflict; 632 buyers surveyed |

Definitions differ between studies, so do not compare the numbers too closely. The direction is consistent. Purchases now cross departments, and buyers consult people outside the company, such as peers, advisers and analysts.

## Why is your champion outnumbered?

Your champion is outnumbered because every stakeholder forms a view of every vendor, and the champion must reconcile all of them. Do the arithmetic. Thirteen internal stakeholders and five vendors make 65 stakeholder-vendor pairs. That is our arithmetic, not a research finding. But it shows the load on one person. Most of those 65 views form in meetings you are not in.

Conflict makes it harder. A Gartner survey of 632 B2B buyers, published in May 2025, found that 74% of buying teams showed unhealthy conflict during the decision. Gartner defines unhealthy conflict as members having conflicting objectives, disagreeing on the best course of action, or being overruled by outside decision-makers. Forrester reported in 2024 that 86% of B2B purchases stall during the buying process.

The disagreement is often about the problem, not the vendor. Finance sees a cost issue. Operations sees a process issue. IT sees a risk. If the group never agrees on what the problem is, no vendor comparison can settle it.

## Why does consensus matter more than the champion?

Consensus matters more because it predicts whether buyers judge the deal a good one. In the same Gartner study, buying groups that reached consensus were 2.5 times more likely to report a high-quality deal. Buyers who experienced buying-group relevance were three times more likely to report a high-quality deal.

Gartner also found a trap. Content tailored to each individual's priorities had a 59% negative impact on buying-group consensus. Tailoring for the group's shared relevance improved consensus by 20%. Personalization that pleases each stakeholder alone can push them apart. The aim is a shared story, with each role's concern answered inside it.

## How do you sell to consensus?

Sell to consensus by getting the group to agree on the problem and its cost before you compare solutions. We use a six-part **consensus kit**:

1. **One problem statement, in their words.** "Your stage-2 drop-off", not "pipeline challenges". It should fit in three sentences.
2. **A cost the CFO recognizes.** Put the problem in money per quarter, using the buyer's own numbers.
3. **The "who else" question, on every call.** "Who else needs to agree with this?" Write the answers into the CRM.
4. **The sponsor by call two.** Ask to meet the economic buyer early, while it is still a normal request.
5. **A phase one that pays back alone.** Value it in money and in the time the buyer's team will spend. Offer a checkpoint after phase one before they ask.
6. **A forwardable one-page case.** The champion must be able to send it without you in the room, with the two or three questions each role will ask already answered.

The realism line: you will not meet all 13 people. The champion has to carry the story to the rest, so make it easy to carry.

## Where do multi-stakeholder deals leak?

Multi-stakeholder deals rarely die at the demo. They leak at quieter moments, and each leak is a skipped conversation:

| Leak | What happens | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Proposal sent by email | Objections land in an inbox you cannot see | Book the walkthrough call before you send the PDF |
| No economic buyer met | The champion is comfortable; you do not push | Ask for the sponsor by the second call |
| Discount with no trade | Value drops and the decision date does not move | Trade for a decision date, a longer term or a reference |
| "Interesting, thanks" | You told them nothing new | Bring one number they have not seen |
| Soft follow-up | "Let me know if you have questions" | End with a date, an owner and a decision |
| Call two drifts | Discovery was good but nobody said the problem back | Open call two with the problem and its cost |

None of these is fixed by a better document. Each needs a named call.

## What does the buyer count that your value case misses?

The buyer counts their team's time. Late in a deal, pushback is often "make it simpler and more relevant", not "lower the price". The value case counts license and services. The buyer counts hours their people spend away from their jobs. The value case shows payback over the full program. The buyer wants to know whether phase one pays back alone, because that is the only promise a sponsor can defend without you. Price phase one on its own, in time as well as money. Some value only appears after the full sequence. Say so, and still price the checkpoint.

## When can an AI agent sell and when does it take a rep?

An AI agent can handle the sale when one person buys and already knows the problem. It needs a rep when many people must agree on a vague problem. Two questions sort deals:

| | Problem already clear | Problem still vague |
|---|---|---|
| **One buyer** | Agent closes: price, sign, start | Agent diagnoses, names the cost, hands off when complex |
| **Many buyers** | Agent builds the case; a rep aligns the group | Human-led: helping the group find and agree on the problem is the sale |

Plot your last ten wins on this grid. Most large deals sit in the bottom-right box. That work does not move to a chatbot when ten people have to agree.

## Example: mapping one deal

Example: a seller's largest open deal is worth $400,000. The CRM shows four contacts. On the next call, the seller asks the champion who else needs to agree. The answer adds eight names across finance, IT, operations and procurement. The seller has met three of the 12. Two are known to doubt the problem exists.

The seller makes three moves. First, a one-page problem statement with the cost: $90,000 a quarter in lost stage-2 conversions, from the buyer's own funnel. Second, a 30-minute review of that page with the champion and the finance lead. Third, a phase-one plan that pays back in two quarters on its own. Coverage rises to 6 of 12 in three weeks. The deal does not close faster yet, but the conflict is now visible and named.

## What should enablement build for buying groups?

Enablement should build for the group, not the persona. In practice:

- A problem-statement template and a one-page case template reps can fill in an hour.
- [AI roleplays](/guides/ai-roleplay-sales-training/) with two or three buyer personas in one meeting, so reps practice handling disagreement.
- A [skills scorecard](/guides/sales-skills-scorecard/) behavior: "confirms who else must agree".
- A CRM field for stakeholders met versus stakeholders named.
- A coaching question for managers: "Who in this deal have you never spoken to?"

See [problem-first selling](/guides/problem-first-selling/) for how to open the conversation that consensus is built on.

## Common mistakes

- **Optimizing for the champion alone.** The champion's enthusiasm does not survive a meeting you are not in.
- **Personalizing for each stakeholder separately.** It can split the group. Build one shared story.
- **Treating multithreading as consensus.** Contacts are not agreement.
- **Emailing the proposal.** Walk it through on a call where you can hear objections.
- **Valuing only the full program.** Price phase one on its own, including the buyer's time.

If you want to know whether your team has the hours to build and coach this, start with a free [Capacity Check](/#capacity-check).

## FAQ

### How many people are in a B2B buying group?

Forrester's State of Business Buying 2026 reports 13 internal stakeholders and nine external influencers in a typical purchase. Its 2024 edition also found 13 people involved on average, with 89% of purchases spanning two or more departments. Definitions differ between studies, but the direction is consistent: ten or more people.

### How many vendors do B2B buyers evaluate?

6sense's 2025 Buyer Experience Report found buyers evaluated an average of about five vendors. The same study found buyers bought from the vendor they ranked first 77% of the time, so the shortlist forms early.

### Why do B2B deals stall even when the champion is keen?

Because the champion is one voice among many. Forrester reported in 2024 that 86% of B2B purchases stall during the buying process, and Gartner found 74% of buying teams show unhealthy conflict. Most stalls come from people disagreeing about the problem, not about your product.

### What is the difference between a champion and an economic buyer?

A champion wants the change and sells it internally. An economic buyer controls the budget and signs. They are often different people, and a deal with a champion but no access to the economic buyer is at risk. Ask to meet the sponsor by the second call.

### How do you build consensus in a buying group you cannot meet?

Make the story easy to carry. Give the champion a one-page problem statement with the cost in the buyer's own numbers, a phase-one plan that pays back on its own, and two or three questions each stakeholder will ask. Then ask the champion who has seen it and what they said.

### Is multithreading the same as selling to consensus?

Not quite. Multithreading means having contacts across the account. Selling to consensus means those contacts agree on the problem, its cost and the path. You can multithread a deal and still lose it to internal conflict.

## Sources

- [Forrester: Forrester's 2026 Buyer Insights: GenAI Is Upending B2B Buying (State of Business Buying, 2026)](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-2026-the-state-of-business-buying/)
- [Forrester: To Master B2B Buying Mayhem, Providers Must Prioritize Buyers' Needs (State of Business Buying, 2024)](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-the-state-of-business-buying-2024/)
- [Gartner: Gartner Sales Survey Finds 74% of B2B Buyer Teams Demonstrate Unhealthy Conflict During the Decision Process (May 2025)](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process)
- [CustomerThink: 6sense Study Provides Critical Insights on B2B Buyer Behavior (2025 Buyer Experience Report)](https://customerthink.com/research-round-up-6sense-study-provides-critical-insights-on-b2b-buyer-behavior/)

# Continuous sales training: why six-week skill sprints beat one-time events

> Continuous sales training replaces one-time workshops with repeating six-week skill sprints: one skill per sprint, scored practice every week, a manager who coaches it on a live deal, and a check of real calls for the behavior. Events end before reps face a real call, so they can only measure attendance. Sprints last long enough to measure behavior.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/continuous-sales-training/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- A one-time training event ends before reps have a real call where the skill matters, so it can only measure attendance.
- A six-week skill sprint focuses on one skill, with scored weekly practice, live-deal coaching and a check of real calls.
- One skill per sprint is a constraint, not a preference: two skills halve the live moments, coaching and evidence for each.
- Our rule: if a skill comes up on fewer than one call a week, practice it in a scored simulation first.
- Research on spaced practice finds that spreading practice over time beats the same practice massed into one block.

A two-day sales workshop can be excellent. The room is engaged, the roleplays are sharp, and the feedback forms are glowing. Then Monday arrives, the pipeline review starts, and nobody mentions the workshop again until next year's refresher. The problem is not the quality of the session. It is the shape. This guide explains why one-time events cannot change behavior, how a six-week skill sprint works, and how to plan a year of them.

## Why do one-time sales training events fail to change behavior?

One-time events fail because they end before the rep has a single real call where the skill matters. So the only things an event can measure are attendance and completion. It cannot see behavior, because no behavior has happened yet.

Memory research explains the rest. Jaap Murre and Joeri Dros replicated Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve in 2015 (PLOS ONE): forgetting is fastest soon after learning and slows over time. Spacing is the counter. A 1999 meta-analysis by John Donovan and David Radosevich in the Journal of Applied Psychology reviewed 63 studies of task performance and found that people who practiced in spaced sessions performed significantly better than those who practiced in one massed block. Nicholas Cepeda and colleagues' 2006 review of 839 assessments (Psychological Bulletin) added a useful rule: the longer you need to remember something, the longer the best gap between practice sessions.

A sales skill must last for years, not for a test on Friday. That argues for practice spread over weeks.

The CSO Insights 2019 Sales Enablement Report makes the business version of the same point: training can start a change, but it needs ongoing coaching to make it effective.

## What is a six-week skill sprint?

A skill sprint is a fixed six-week period focused on one sales skill, owned by front-line managers and measured on real calls. When the sprint ends, the data picks the next gap. The loop has six steps:

1. **Pick one skill.** Choose it from evidence: call reviews, deal losses, roleplay scores.
2. **Diagnose who needs it, by cohort.** Score a baseline by team, region or tenure, not as one organization-wide average. The org may be fine at negotiation while one region is not.
3. **Practice it in a scored simulation.** One short roleplay a week, scored 0 to 100, with a benchmark line.
4. **Watch real calls.** Did the behavior show up where the moment arose?
5. **Coach one live deal.** Each manager coaches the skill on one real opportunity per rep.
6. **Review and pick the next gap.** Compare end scores and call evidence with the baseline, then choose the next sprint's skill.

Between sprints, keep the call signals running, like a quarterly business review for skills. See the [glossary entry for skill sprint](/glossary/#skill-sprint).

## Why only one skill per sprint?

One skill per sprint is a constraint, not a preference. The moments where a skill can be used on a real call are limited. Split a sprint across two skills and each one gets half the live moments, half the coaching and half the evidence.

Do the arithmetic. A rep has about 5 customer calls a week. Over six weeks, that is 30 calls. If the moment for a skill appears on 1 call in 10, the rep gets 3 real chances in the whole sprint. Three attempts is not practice. It is three exams.

## How many live chances does your target skill get?

Count the moments before you plan the coaching. Our rule: if a skill comes up on fewer than one call a week, practice it in a scored simulation first, and save live calls for coaching the moments that do happen. The frequencies below are illustrative. Your call data will give the real numbers, and they vary a lot by skill.

| Skill | Illustrative frequency | Live chances in a 6-week sprint (30 calls) | Where to practice first |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ask a strong follow-up question | Most calls | 25+ | Live calls, with manager review |
| Say the buyer's problem back at the start of call two | 1 in 3 calls | About 10 | Live calls plus weekly roleplay |
| Get the buyer to name the cost of the problem | 1 in 10 calls | About 3 | Scored simulation first |
| Handle a procurement discount push | 1 in 20 calls | 1 or 2 | Scored simulation first |
| Respond to a competitor's price comparison | 1 in 15 calls | About 2 | Scored simulation first |

Rare, high-stakes skills need repetitions somewhere safe. Frequent skills can be learned live.

## A six-week sprint calendar

| Week | What happens | Who | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Week 0 | Pick the skill. Score a baseline by cohort from calls and one roleplay. | Enablement, sales leader | Baseline score and call rate |
| Week 1 | Manager announces the focus skill. First scored roleplay. | Managers, reps | Practice started |
| Weeks 2–5 | One scored roleplay a week. One live-deal coaching session per rep. Weekly manager list. | Reps, managers | Score trend, coaching coverage |
| Week 4 | Mid-sprint check: who is below the line after two attempts? | Enablement, managers | Escalation list |
| Week 6 | Final roleplay. Sample real calls for the behavior. | Enablement | End score, call rate against baseline |
| Week 7 | Review results with the sales leader. Pick the next skill. | Enablement, sales leader | One-page sprint summary |

At six weeks plus one week of review, a team runs about seven sprints a year. Most teams should plan only the first three and let the data pick the rest.

## Skill sprint vs one-time training event

| Dimension | One-time event | Six-week skill sprint |
|---|---|---|
| Duration | 1–2 days | 6 weeks, repeated |
| Skills covered | Many | One |
| Practice | In the room, once | Weekly, scored |
| Manager's role | Attends or approves | Owns coaching and the weekly question |
| What it can measure | Attendance, satisfaction, quiz scores | Practice scores, behavior on calls, early deal movement |
| Main risk | Forgotten by next month | Needs a manager who shows up every week |

## How do you pick the skill for each sprint?

Pick the skill where four tests overlap, scoring each from 1 to 3 and choosing the highest total:

1. **Gap:** roleplay scores or call reviews show a clear gap in at least one cohort.
2. **Leak:** the skill sits at the deal stage where most opportunities stall or are lost.
3. **Visible:** you can observe it, on calls or in a scored simulation.
4. **Coachable:** managers can recognize it and coach it in a 30-minute conversation.

A skill that scores high on the gap but low on visibility, such as overall "executive presence", makes a poor sprint. Break it into something you can hear, such as opening a senior meeting with the buyer's problem in the first two minutes.

## Example: one sprint on "name the cost of the problem"

Example: a team of 80 reps runs a sprint on getting the buyer to name the cost of the problem. In the baseline, the behavior appears on 15% of the calls where the moment arose, and the average roleplay score is 58 against a line of 70. Because the moment arises on only about 1 call in 10, the team leads with weekly simulation.

Over six weeks, 68 reps (85%) complete at least four of the six scored roleplays. The average score rises to 74. Managers log a live-deal coaching session for 60 reps (75%). At week 6, a sample of calls where the moment arose shows the behavior on 35% of them, up from 15%. One region stays at 18%, so the next sprint keeps the same skill for that cohort only, while the rest of the team moves on.

The sprint cost about 60 enablement hours: 20 to build the roleplay and scorecard, 6 a week for lists, scoring and call sampling, and 4 for the review.

## When is a training event still the right choice?

Events still work for launching something new, building energy and bringing people together. A kickoff or a product launch is a good start for a sprint. The mistake is treating the event as the whole program. See the [90-day plan after a sales kickoff](/guides/sales-kickoff-follow-up/) for how to turn an event into the first sprint.

## Common mistakes

- **Covering more skills to look efficient.** Three skills a month feels productive and produces no evidence for any of them.
- **Picking the skill from a wish list.** Pick it from call data and roleplay scores, by cohort.
- **Skipping the baseline.** Without a week-0 number, the week-6 number proves nothing.
- **Running sprints without managers.** Without a weekly manager, a sprint becomes six weeks of reminder emails.

## What are the limits of skill sprints?

The biggest limit is the manager. A sprint needs a manager who shows up every week; if you cannot get that, fix it first with the [six manager jobs](/guides/sales-manager-reinforcement/). Second, some skills barely show up on live calls. For those, lean on simulation and accept slower evidence. Third, behavior evidence needs recorded calls or structured manager observation. And the spacing research cited here comes mostly from lab and task studies, not sales floors, so treat it as a strong direction, not a precise prescription. A shared [sales skills scorecard](/guides/sales-skills-scorecard/) keeps sprints comparable over a year.

If you want to know whether your team has the hours to run continuous sprints, start with a free [20-minute Capacity Check](/#capacity-check).

## FAQ

### What is continuous sales training?

It is training delivered as a repeating cycle rather than a single event. Reps practice one skill at a time, every week, with a score, and managers coach it on real deals. The cycle then picks the next skill based on data.

### What is a skill sprint?

A skill sprint is a fixed period, usually six weeks, focused on one sales skill. It includes a baseline, weekly scored practice, one live-deal coaching session per rep and a check of real calls at the end. The results choose the next sprint's skill.

### Why six weeks?

Six weeks gives a rep about 30 customer calls at five a week, enough for a common skill to show up several times on real calls. It is also short enough to hold one focus. Shorter sprints rarely produce call evidence; longer ones lose attention.

### How often should sales reps practice?

Weekly, with a score, during an active sprint. Spaced practice research finds that sessions spread over time beat the same amount of practice crammed into one block. One 15-minute scored roleplay a week is a realistic floor.

### Are sales training events still useful?

Yes, for launching something new, building energy and bringing people together. They work best as the start of a sprint, not as the whole program.

### How many skill sprints can a team run in a year?

About seven or eight, if each sprint is six weeks with a one-week gap for review and planning. Most teams should pick their first three from data, not from a wish list.

## Sources

- [Journal of Applied Psychology: Donovan and Radosevich, A Meta-Analytic Review of the Distribution of Practice Effect (1999)](https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.84.5.795)
- [Psychological Bulletin: Cepeda et al., Distributed Practice in Verbal Recall Tasks (2006)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16719566/)
- [PLOS ONE: Murre and Dros, Replication and Analysis of Ebbinghaus' Forgetting Curve (2015)](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0120644)
- [CSO Insights (Miller Heiman Group): 2019 Sales Enablement Report](https://community.highspot.com/assets/2019/10/CSO-Insights-5th-Annual-Sales-Enablement-Study.pdf)

# Cost per active user: the enablement tool metric to check before renewal

> Cost per active user is the annual license cost of an enablement tool divided by the number of reps who logged in and completed something in the last 30 days. Check it before every renewal. If it is more than 2.5 times the price per seat, fewer than 40% of seats are active.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/cost-per-active-user/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- Cost per active user = annual license cost ÷ reps who logged in and completed something in the last 30 days.
- Divide cost per active user by the price per seat to get the multiple: under 1.4x is healthy, 1.4x to 2.5x needs watching, above 2.5x needs action.
- Low usage rarely means a bad tool; it usually means nobody had the hours to fill it, launch programs in it and chase completion.
- Before a renewal, ask what it would take to double the number of active users, not which tool to switch to.

Every enablement tool has a renewal date, and most renewal conversations start with the wrong number: the price per seat. The number that matters is what each rep who actually uses the tool costs you. This guide gives you the formula, thresholds, a worked example across three tools and a plan for when the number is high.

## What is cost per active user?

[Cost per active user](/glossary/#cost-per-active-user) is the annual license cost of a tool divided by the number of reps who used it in the last 30 days.

**Cost per active user = annual license cost ÷ reps who logged in and completed something in the last 30 days**

"Completed something" is the important part. A login with no action is not use. Define one meaningful action per tool:

- **[LMS](/glossary/#lms):** finished a module, assessment or certification step.
- **Content platform:** opened assigned content or shared content with a buyer.
- **Roleplay or practice tool:** completed a scored practice session.

Exclude admins, enablement staff and test accounts. Include managers only if the tool is meant for them.

## How do you calculate cost per active user?

You need two numbers and about ten minutes.

1. **Annual cost.** Take the full annual contract value, including add-on modules and premium support. If you paid for implementation, spread it over the contract term.
2. **Active reps.** Export usage for the last 30 days. Count unique reps with at least one meaningful action.
3. **Divide** annual cost by active reps.
4. **Calculate the multiple.** Divide cost per active user by the price per seat (annual cost ÷ seats bought). The multiple equals seats bought ÷ active reps, so it shows how far usage falls short of what you pay for.

The [cost per active user calculator](/tools/cost-per-active-user-calculator/) does steps 3 and 4 for several tools at once.

## Example: three enablement tools, one renewal season

Example: a company with 400 reps runs three enablement tools.

| Tool | Annual cost | Seats | Price per seat | Active in last 30 days | Active rate | Cost per active user | Multiple |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LMS | $48,000 | 400 | $120 | 280 | 70% | $171 | 1.4x |
| Content platform | $90,000 | 400 | $225 | 160 | 40% | $563 | 2.5x |
| Roleplay tool | $75,000 | 250 | $300 | 50 | 20% | $1,500 | 5.0x |

The company spends $213,000 a year on these three tools. The idle seats cost $128,400 of it: 120 LMS seats ($14,400), 240 content platform seats ($54,000) and 200 roleplay seats ($60,000). That is 60% of the spend.

The price per seat looked reasonable in every case. The cost per active user tells a different story. Each rep who practiced in the roleplay tool last month cost $1,500 a year.

## What thresholds should you use?

Use the multiple, because it works for any price. These are our working thresholds, not a published standard.

| Multiple (cost per active user ÷ price per seat) | Active rate | Status | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Under 1.4x | 70% or more | Healthy | Keep running; check content freshness each quarter |
| 1.4x to 2.5x | 40% to 70% | Watch | Find which teams are inactive and why |
| Above 2.5x | Under 40% | Act | Run a 90-day operations plan before renewal |

For context across all software, not only enablement: Zylo's 2026 SaaS Management Index data shows the average organization uses 54% of its provisioned licenses. That is a multiple of about 1.85x. Enablement tools that every rep is meant to use should do better.

**One adjustment for burst tools.** Some tools are used in waves: onboarding modules by new hires, certification tools around a launch. For these, divide by the reps who were assigned work in the window, or use a 90-day window. Otherwise a well-run onboarding tool will look idle in a month with no new hires.

## Why is cost per active user high?

Low usage rarely means a bad tool. It usually means nobody had the hours to fill the tool with current content, build programs in it, launch them properly and chase completion. The tool was bought; the operations were not.

Enablement leaders know this pattern. They were sold a platform and handed a second job: running it. The public data points the same way. In the 2025 Impact of Enablement report from Spekit and the Sales Enablement Collective, 80% of enablement professionals said reps do not use at least 40% of their platform's features, and 48.8% said at least 40% of their collateral is out of date. (The report was co-produced by a platform vendor, so read it as directional.)

There is a cost on the rep side too. Gartner's 2024 survey of 1,026 B2B sellers found that 50% feel overwhelmed by the amount of technology their job needs, and Gartner reported that overwhelmed sellers are 45% less likely to attain quota. A half-used tool is not neutral. It is one more login competing for attention.

Check these causes in order, cheapest first:

| Cause | Sign | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| No assigned work | Reps have nothing due in the tool | Launch one program with a deadline |
| Stale or empty content | Top assets are over six months old | Refresh the ten most-used assets |
| No manager ask | Managers never mention the tool in one-to-ones | Send each manager a weekly list of who has not started |
| Outside the workflow | Reps must leave the CRM or chat tool to use it | Add links or integrations where reps already work |
| Too many seats | Seats were bought for future headcount | Right-size at renewal |
| Poor fit | Usage stays low after all of the above | Consolidate or replace |

Most teams find the cause in the first three rows. The manager row matters most. When managers reinforce a program, usage rises. When they do not, even a well-built program fades. See [why training fades without managers](/guides/sales-manager-reinforcement/).

## What should you do when cost per active user is high?

Ask what it would take to double the number of active users, not which tool to switch to. Switching tools resets the content, the integrations and the habits, and the operations gap moves with you.

A 90-day plan before renewal:

1. **Days 1–15:** Load or refresh the content reps need for one live priority, such as a launch or a quarter-end play.
2. **Days 15–30:** Launch one program in the tool with a message from the sales leader and a clear deadline.
3. **Days 30–90:** Nudge reps who have not started. Send managers their list each week. Escalate teams below target to the sales leader.
4. **Day 90:** Recalculate cost per active user and decide.

Applied to the roleplay tool in the example, you face a real choice. Cut to 75 seats (50 active plus a buffer) and pay about $22,500 for 50 practicing reps. Or keep 250 seats, run the plan and reach 150 active reps at $500 each. The second option costs more and produces three times the practice. Which is right depends on whether practice in that tool is tied to a priority behavior. See [AI roleplay for sales training](/guides/ai-roleplay-sales-training/) for the conditions under which practice pays back.

## How do you use cost per active user in a renewal?

Bring three numbers to the renewal: cost per active user today, the active-user target for next year, and the seat count that target needs plus a growth buffer. Ask the vendor what adoption support is included. Ask for a seat count that steps up as usage grows, rather than paying today for next year's headcount. Note that per-seat prices often rise at lower volumes, so compare total cost, not only the multiple.

## What are the limits of this metric?

Cost per active user measures use, not value. A rep who opens a battlecard every day is active; whether the battlecard helped win the deal is a separate question that needs behavior and outcome data. It also depends on login data, which is changing: as AI agents do more work inside sales tools, logins will understate use. When that happens, divide by completed outcomes instead, such as reps certified or practice sessions scored. The [sales enablement ROI guide](/guides/sales-enablement-roi/) shows how to do that across the whole budget.

## Common mistakes

- **Counting logins as use.** Require one completed action per rep.
- **Calculating it the week before renewal.** Start 90 days ahead, so there is time to act.
- **Blaming the tool first.** Check assigned work, content and manager asks before you switch.
- **Buying seats for next year's headcount.** Pay for active use plus a buffer, and step up as you hire.
- **Using a 30-day window for burst tools.** Measure onboarding and certification tools against the reps who had work assigned.

If your tools are half-used because the hours to run them do not exist, the free [20-minute Capacity Check](/#capacity-check) estimates how many hours your plan needs.

## FAQ

### What counts as an active user?

A rep who logged in and completed a meaningful action in the last 30 days: finished a module or assessment in the LMS, opened or shared assigned content in the content platform, or completed a scored session in a roleplay tool. A login with no completed action does not count. Admins and enablement staff should be excluded.

### What is a good active user rate for a sales enablement tool?

Our working threshold is 70% or more of licensed reps active in a 30-day window for tools every rep should use, such as a content platform. For tools used in bursts, such as onboarding modules, measure against the reps who were assigned work in that period instead of all seats.

### Is cost per active user the same as cost per license?

No. Cost per license divides cost by seats bought. Cost per active user divides cost by seats actually used. When every seat is active, the two match. When half the seats are idle, cost per active user is double the cost per license.

### How often should you calculate cost per active user?

Monthly is enough to see a trend, and it takes minutes once the usage export is set up. At a minimum, calculate it 90 days before each renewal, so there is time to run an adoption plan or renegotiate seats before the deadline.

### Should we cancel a tool with a high cost per active user?

Not first. Check whether the tool has current content, an assigned program with a deadline, and managers who ask about it. If none of those exist, fix them for 90 days and measure again. Cancel or consolidate if usage stays low after the operations are in place.

### How does AI affect cost per active user?

As AI agents do more work inside sales tools on a rep's behalf, logins may fall even when the tool is delivering value. In that case, count completed outcomes, such as certified reps or practice sessions, instead of logins, and keep the same formula.

## Sources

- [Zylo: Tracking employee SaaS usage uncovers significant underutilization (2026 SaaS Management Index data)](https://zylo.com/blog/saas-usage-numbers)
- [Newswire (Spekit and Sales Enablement Collective): New research reveals the hidden cost of traditional enablement platforms, 2025 Impact of Enablement report](https://www.newswire.com/news/new-research-reveals-the-hidden-cost-of-traditional-enablement-22554701)
- [Gartner: Gartner sales survey reveals sellers who partner with AI are 3.7 times more likely to meet quota (September 2024)](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2024-09-16-gartner-sales-survey-reveals-sellers-who-partner-with-ai-re-three-point-seven-times-more-likely-to-meet-quota)

# How to design a sales enablement pilot that answers the scale question

> Design a sales enablement pilot around the question it must answer, then size it. A readiness pilot of 15–30 reps tests logistics. A proof pilot needs enough reps to compare groups, usually 100 or more, a pre-launch baseline, a team that starts 30 days later, agreed data access and a scale rule written down before launch.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/enablement-pilot-design/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- Pilot size is a design decision: decide what the pilot must prove before you choose how many reps to include.
- A readiness pilot tests whether people finish and what breaks; a proof pilot tests whether behavior and outcomes change enough to scale.
- With 25 reps, the margin of error on a 30% rate is about plus or minus 18 points, too wide to rank teams.
- Low pilot completion is usually a sponsor-network problem, not a content problem; name the three peer leaders the sponsor will enlist.
- Report week-2 usage against week 1, and relaunch fixes personally to the reps the first version lost.

Pilots get kept small to lower the risk. Then a skeptical sales leader asks whether the program works at 100 reps or more, and the pilot has no answer either way. The risk you avoided by keeping it small comes back as doubt. This guide shows how to design a pilot that answers the question the scale decision depends on.

## What question must the pilot answer?

Decide what the pilot must prove before you decide its size. There are two kinds of pilot, and most failed pilots are one kind sold as the other.

| | Readiness pilot | Proof pilot |
|---|---|---|
| Question | Can we run it? Do people finish? What breaks? | Does it change behavior and outcomes enough to scale? |
| Typical size | 15–30 reps, one or two teams | 100 or more reps, several teams |
| Length | 2–4 weeks | 60–90 days |
| Comparison group | Not needed | A team that starts later, or a holdout |
| Main metrics | Completion, week-2 usage, support load, time per session | Behavior rate vs baseline, outcome at the target stage |
| Output | A fix list | A scale, extend or stop decision |

A small pilot is still useful. It shows logistics, support load and whether people finish. Call it a readiness pilot and do not let anyone read it as proof.

## How big does a proof pilot need to be?

Big enough that the difference you care about is larger than the noise. The quick check is the margin of error on a rate:

**95% margin of error ≈ 1.96 × √(p × (1 − p) ÷ n)**

where p is the rate you expect (for example, the share of reps who show a behavior) and n is the number of reps.

| Reps in the group (n) | Margin on a 30% rate |
|---|---|
| 5 | ± 40 points |
| 25 | ± 18 points |
| 100 | ± 9 points |
| 400 | ± 4.5 points |

A 25-rep pilot split across five teams gives five reps a team. At that size, a team's rate could sit anywhere in an 80-point range by chance. The results still get ranked, and the "top" team is really just the least weak. The report reads like a verdict, but it is noise.

This is not only a sales problem. A widely cited review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience showed that small studies have a reduced chance of detecting a true effect, and that low power also makes significant results less likely to be true and tends to inflate effect sizes ([Button et al., 2013](https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/en/publications/power-failure-why-small-sample-size-undermines-the-reliability-of/)). A small pilot that "worked" may have worked less than it looked.

Our rule of thumb: below roughly 100 people, present pooled results with a caveat and do not rank groups. The formula also flatters you, because reps on the same team are not independent. Real margins are wider.

## How do you build a comparison group without holding anyone back?

Use a staggered start. All teams begin without the program, then switch to it in waves, typically 30 days apart. Until a team switches, it serves as the comparison for the teams that already have.

Health researchers use the same design, called a stepped wedge trial. In it, all clusters start in the control condition and a random order decides when each one crosses over ([Campbell, Hemming and Taljaard, 2019](https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2019/210/6/stepped-wedge-cluster-randomised-trial-what-it-and-when-it-should-be-used)). The same paper names the main risk: confounding by time. A new pricing change or a strong month lands on everyone, so always compare waves in the same calendar period, never wave 1's first month against wave 2's first month.

Three rules make it fair:

1. Use waves of similar size, segment and tenure.
2. Decide the order by coin flip, not by which manager is keenest.
3. Take the baseline for every wave before wave 1 starts. Gartner's guidance is the same: establish a baseline for the targeted behaviors before you try to show impact ([Gartner, 2023](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2023-02-15-gartner-expects-sales-enablement-budgets-to-increase-by-50-percent-by-2027)).

## What must be agreed before launch?

Agree three things in writing: the data, the metrics and the decision rule.

- **Data.** Who supplies call and CRM data, in what format, by what date, and where it will be analyzed. If someone names an outcome metric but never sends the data, the pilot is a demo, not a test. Call data access is often a legal and IT conversation, so start it in week one.
- **Metrics.** One behavior metric, one usage metric and one outcome metric, each with a formula. The [sales enablement metrics guide](/guides/sales-enablement-metrics/) lists formulas for each level.
- **Decision rule.** What result means scale, extend or stop. Write it before you see any data.

## Why do pilots stall, and how do you prevent it?

Low pilot completion is usually a network problem, not a content problem. When a pilot stalls, the first explanation is always the content. Peel it back and the pattern is often the same. Reps say they are too busy. Their managers never mentioned it. The peer leaders who run those teams were never told the pilot existed. And the sponsor is isolated, often new in the role and without the standing to call in favors yet.

Change research backs the sponsor's role. Prosci's Best Practices in Change Management report has found active and visible sponsorship to be the top contributor to success since 1998. In its 12th edition, projects with extremely effective sponsors met objectives 79% of the time, against 27% with extremely ineffective sponsors ([Prosci](https://www.prosci.com/resources/articles/change-management-best-practices)).

Before launch, ask one question: which three peer leaders will the sponsor personally enlist? If the answer is unclear, that is the plan. A brand-new sponsor is not a neutral fact; it is a risk factor. The fix is cheap once named: brief the peer leaders and, if needed, reopen the window. Managers matter one level down, too; see [why training fades without managers](/guides/sales-manager-reinforcement/).

## How should you report pilot usage?

Report week 2 against week 1, not a cumulative total. Week 1 measures the announcement. Week 2 measures the program. A launch total hides the most useful number in the chart, which is how much usage survives when nobody is pushing.

**Retention ratio = reps active in week 2 ÷ reps active in week 1.**

Plot it weekly for the whole pilot. A falling ratio in week 2 is a design signal; a falling ratio in week 5 is often a manager signal.

## Is a fix the same as a relaunch?

No. Reps decide once. A fix shipped quietly reaches nobody who already left, and partial coverage trains the habit of not using the tool. This is common with new tools for sellers: version one covers half the workflow, reps use it until their deal moves past that half, then stop. The rest ships later, and they do not come back.

Three habits help. Ship the whole workflow thinly before any stage deeply. When a fix lands, relaunch it personally to the reps the first version lost; release notes are not a relaunch. And if you cannot wait for full coverage, say plainly which deals it is for and give a date for the rest. This applies with special force to [AI roleplay pilots](/guides/ai-roleplay-sales-training/), where first impressions of a clunky session last.

## Example: a 120-rep proof pilot

Example: a company wants to know whether a discovery program should go to all 600 reps. It designs a proof pilot with 120 reps in two waves of 60. Wave 1 starts on 12 January, wave 2 on 9 February. Baselines for both waves are taken in the two weeks before 12 January.

The decision rule, written before launch: scale if, by 8 February, the share of reps showing the behavior on most eligible calls rose at least 10 points more in wave 1 than in wave 2, and the week-2 retention ratio was at least 60%. These thresholds are an example, not a standard.

| Metric | Wave 1 baseline | Wave 1, 8 Feb | Wave 2 baseline | Wave 2, 8 Feb |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Reps showing the behavior on most eligible calls | 25% | 45% | 25% | 27% |
| Active reps, week 1 → week 2 | n/a | 54 → 41 | n/a | n/a |

Wave 1 rose 20 points and wave 2 rose 2, a difference of 18 points. With 60 reps per wave, the margin on each rate is roughly ± 12 points, so an 18-point gap is unlikely to be chance; a 5-point gap would not be. The retention ratio is 41 ÷ 54, or 76%. Both conditions pass, so the program scales in waves of 120, keeping the staggered design. Results go onto the [monthly CRO report](/guides/enablement-report-for-cro/).

## Common mistakes

- **Sizing for low risk instead of for the question.** The skeptic's question goes unanswered.
- **Ranking teams of five.** The "winner" is noise.
- **No baseline.** Nothing to compare against, so every result is an opinion.
- **No data agreement.** The outcome metric is named and never delivered.
- **Launching through one contact.** Completion follows the sponsor's network, not the quality of the content.

The limit: even a well-designed proof pilot shows that a program works in your conditions this quarter. It does not guarantee the effect holds at ten times the size without the operations behind it.

If you are deciding whether you have the hours to run a pilot like this properly, the free 20-minute [Capacity Check](/#capacity-check) is a useful first conversation.

## FAQ

### How long should a sales enablement pilot run?

A readiness pilot needs two to four weeks. A proof pilot needs 60 to 90 days: about two weeks for baseline, 30 days for the first wave before the comparison team starts, and enough time for behavior to show on calls. Outcome metrics may need a full cycle at the target stage.

### How many reps do you need for a sales pilot?

For a readiness pilot, 15 to 30 reps across one or two teams is enough. For a proof pilot that compares groups, plan for 100 or more, split into groups of at least 25 to 30. Below roughly 100 people, report pooled results with a caveat and do not rank teams.

### What success criteria should a sales pilot have?

Write them before launch: the behavior metric and the minimum change that counts, the usage threshold, the outcome you will watch and who supplies the data. Add the decision each result triggers, such as scale, extend or stop.

### Why do sales enablement pilots fail?

Most fail on design rather than content: too small to compare groups, no baseline, no agreed data or a sponsor without a network to drive completion. A pilot that cannot answer the skeptic's question has failed even if everyone liked it.

### Should a vendor tool pilot use your own data?

Yes, if the pilot is meant to prove impact. If the outcome metric is named but the data never arrives, the pilot is a demo, not a test. Agree access with legal and IT before kickoff, including where the data is analyzed.

### What happens after a successful pilot?

Scale in waves, not all at once. Keep the staggered-start design so each new wave has a comparison, keep the same metric definitions and relaunch to any pilot reps who dropped off. Budget the operations work, not just the licenses.

## Sources

- [Button et al., Power failure: why small sample size undermines the reliability of neuroscience, Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2013)](https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/en/publications/power-failure-why-small-sample-size-undermines-the-reliability-of/)
- [Campbell, Hemming and Taljaard, The stepped wedge cluster randomised trial: what it is and when it should be used, Medical Journal of Australia (2019)](https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2019/210/6/stepped-wedge-cluster-randomised-trial-what-it-and-when-it-should-be-used)
- [Prosci: Best practices in change management](https://www.prosci.com/resources/articles/change-management-best-practices)
- [Gartner: Gartner expects sales enablement budgets to increase by 50% by 2027 (press release, February 2023)](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2023-02-15-gartner-expects-sales-enablement-budgets-to-increase-by-50-percent-by-2027)

# The one-page monthly enablement report a CRO will actually read

> A monthly enablement report a CRO will read fits on one page. It opens with one sentence on what changed and what decision is needed, then shows four levels of evidence: activity, practice, behavior on real calls and the outcome at the target stage. Each number sits next to its pre-launch baseline and, where possible, a team that started later.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/enablement-report-for-cro/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- A CRO reads an enablement report that answers one question: are more sellers doing the things that move quota?
- Put the four levels of evidence on one page: activity, practice, behavior on real calls and the outcome at the target stage.
- Every number needs its pre-launch baseline beside it, and ideally a comparison team that started 30 days later.
- Open with a single headline sentence and end with no more than two decisions you need from the CRO.
- Name one owner for the chain from training to behavior to quota, or the report will keep stopping at completion.

Enablement reports what happened. The CRO asked what changed. That gap explains why so many monthly reports go unread: completion at 94%, attendance up, content views up, and nothing that answers the question a CRO funds, which is whether more sellers will hit quota. This guide gives you a one-page template, a formula for the headline and a filled-in example.

## Why don't CROs read most enablement reports?

CROs skip most enablement reports because the reports stop at activity. Completion and attendance prove the training was delivered. They say nothing about whether a rep did anything differently on Tuesday's call.

The root cause is ownership, not data. Training sits with enablement, behavior sits with frontline managers and quota sits with sales leadership. Nobody owns the hand-off between them, so each piece gets reported alone. The first fix is not a better dashboard. It is naming one owner for the chain from training to quota. If that answer takes more than five seconds, that is the problem.

The reverse error also costs trust. Gartner found that more than two-thirds of enablement leaders measure their impact by pipeline conversion rates, which enablement has little direct effect on ([Gartner](https://www.gartner.com/en/sales/trends/sales-enablement-metrics)). A report that claims whole-funnel numbers gets challenged, and the CRO stops reading the rest.

The upside is real. Forrester's 2025 B2B Sales Survey found that high-performing sales teams were 37% more likely to measure enablement's impact on the wider organization ([Forrester, 2026](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/from-dread-to-confidence-what-a-live-experiment-revealed-about-revenue-enablements-secret-powers/)).

## What goes on the one page?

The page has seven blocks, in this order. Each block answers one question in no more than three lines.

| Block | Question it answers | What goes in it |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Headline | What changed, and what do you need? | One sentence: behavior, outcome, decision |
| 2. Activity | Did reps complete it? | On-time completion and active users, by team |
| 3. Practice | Can they do it when asked? | Weekly practice rate, share of reps scoring 70 or above |
| 4. Behavior | Do they do it on real calls? | Behavior rate on eligible calls, coaching coverage |
| 5. Outcome | Did the target stage move? | One outcome metric at the stage the behavior affects |
| 6. Next month | What will enablement change? | Two or three actions, each with an owner |
| 7. Decisions | What do you need from the CRO? | No more than two, each answerable yes or no |

Under blocks 2 to 5, use one numbers grid. Keep the columns fixed every month so trends read at a glance.

| Metric | Baseline (before launch) | Last month | This month | Comparison team | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| On-time completion | n/a | | | | |
| Weekly practice rate | | | | | |
| Share at or above 70 | | | | | |
| Behavior rate on eligible calls | | | | | |
| Coaching coverage | | | | | |
| Outcome at target stage | | | | | |

Status is one word: on track, watch or off track. Where calls are not recorded, label the behavior row with its source, such as roleplay scores or manager observations. The [four levels of evidence](/glossary/#four-levels-of-evidence) explain each row, and the [sales enablement metrics guide](/guides/sales-enablement-metrics/) gives the formulas.

## How do you write the headline sentence?

Write the headline as behavior, then outcome, then decision. The formula:

**"[Behavior] rose from [baseline] to [now] in [team]; [outcome] moved [X points] against [comparison]; we need [decision]."**

If the outcome has not moved yet, say so and say when it will be readable. A CRO trusts "too early to read, we will know by 15 January" more than a soft claim.

## How do you show cause without overclaiming?

Show cause with two things set up before launch: a baseline and a comparison. Gartner's guidance is that sales leaders must first establish a baseline for the targeted behaviors, so changed behaviors can be compared against it ([Gartner, 2023](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2023-02-15-gartner-expects-sales-enablement-budgets-to-increase-by-50-percent-by-2027)). For the comparison, start one team 30 days before a similar team. For that month, the later team shows what would have happened anyway.

Agree the outcome with the CRO before the program starts. Kirkpatrick Partners calls this return on expectations: key stakeholders define what success means in advance, instead of the evaluator picking a metric afterward ([Kirkpatrick Partners](https://www.kirkpatrickpartners.com/the-kirkpatrick-model/)). A CRO who chose the metric reads the report.

## Example: a filled-in October report

Example: a company runs a program on price conversations, with the target behavior "trade every concession for something in return." East region (60 reps) started on 1 September. West region (60 reps) starts on 1 November, so for September and October West is the comparison group. Behavior is scored on calls and on a sample of email threads, because many concessions happen in email.

**Headline:** Traded concessions rose from 30% to 48% of eligible deals in East, against 28% to 29% in West, which has not started; median discount at close fell 3 points in East and 1 point in West; we need a weekly coaching slot for East managers before West launches.

| Metric | East baseline | East October | West baseline | West October | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| On-time completion | n/a | 92% | n/a | Not started | On track |
| Weekly practice rate | 0% | 38% | 0% | 0% | Watch (target 50%) |
| Share at or above 70 | 22% | 51% | 20% | 21% | On track |
| Concessions traded, eligible deals | 30% | 48% | 28% | 29% | On track |
| Coaching coverage | 40% | 55% | 38% | 39% | Off track (target 70%) |
| Median discount at close | 14% | 11% | 15% | 14% | Watch |

**Next month:** launch West on 1 November with a message from the regional sales leader (owner: enablement); send East managers the list of reps with no coaching record (owner: enablement); pull November discount data on 3 December (owner: RevOps).

**Decision:** approve a 15-minute coaching slot in every regional manager's weekly meeting from November. Yes or no.

The behavior effect is 18 points in East minus 1 point in West, or 17 points, which is clear. The discount row is marked "watch," not "on track." Two months of closed deals is too few to separate a 2-point difference from normal variation, and the report says so.

## What makes the report better every month?

The report gets better when it is fed by a loop, not a one-off data pull. A call happens and is tied to a deal stage. One named behavior is scored 0 to 100. The manager coaches that behavior for a week. The next call is scored on the same skill. What the top scorers do differently goes into the playbook, and the rubric improves.

Over time the asset is not the course. It is the scored call history. The loop rarely stalls at the scoring step. It stalls when someone has to rewrite the playbook, which is a human job that needs a named owner. Put that owner on the report. The [sales skills scorecard](/guides/sales-skills-scorecard/) and [coaching coverage](/guides/sales-coaching-coverage/) guides cover the two inputs.

## How should the report handle a program that is not working?

Report it on the same page, in the same format, with a recommendation. A report that only shows green rows stops being believed. One red row, explained, builds more trust than six green ones.

Three signals usually show a program in trouble before outcomes do:

- **Week-2 usage falls far below week 1.** Week 1 measures the announcement. Week 2 measures the program. Report the ratio, week-2 active reps ÷ week-1 active reps, not the launch total.
- **Weekly practice stalls below 25%** (our rule of thumb) while completion looks fine. Reps are clicking through, not practicing.
- **Coaching coverage stays flat.** Managers have not picked it up, and behavior will fade.

For each, offer one of three decisions: fix and relaunch to the reps it lost, narrow it to the teams where it works, or stop it and move the hours elsewhere.

## How long does the report take each month?

About one day of work once the joins exist. A workable rhythm:

1. **Working day 1–3:** RevOps pulls CRM outcomes; enablement pulls completion, practice and scorecard data.
2. **Day 4:** enablement writes the headline and the next-month actions.
3. **Day 5:** a 20-to-30-minute review with the CRO, page on screen, decisions taken in the room.

The first month takes longer, because the join between training records and call evidence has to be built. Call data access is often a legal and IT conversation, so start it early.

## Common mistakes

- **Leading with completion.** It belongs on the page, never in the headline.
- **No baseline.** Without it, every number is just a number.
- **Too many programs on one page.** Report the two or three that matter; list the rest by name only.
- **Decisions buried at the bottom.** Put them in the headline and repeat them in block 7.
- **Reporting individual reps.** Report teams and cohorts; keep individual results in coaching.

The limit: one page will not prove a perfect causal link from a module to a closed deal. It can show a believable chain, month after month, and that is what earns the next budget. If you are planning a new program, design the test first with the [enablement pilot guide](/guides/enablement-pilot-design/).

If producing this page every month is the part your team never has hours for, the free 20-minute [Capacity Check](/#capacity-check) will show where the time could come from.

## FAQ

### What should a sales enablement report include?

A one-sentence headline, one or two metrics at each of the four levels of evidence (activity, practice, behavior, outcome), the baseline for each, a comparison team where you have one, what you will change next month and up to two decisions you need from leadership.

### How often should enablement report to the CRO?

Monthly, on one page, with a short live review of 20 to 30 minutes. Add a quarterly review that looks at trends across programs and resets priorities. Weekly reporting is too noisy for behavior and outcome metrics.

### Who should own the monthly enablement report?

The head of enablement should own it, with RevOps supplying CRM data and frontline managers supplying coaching records. One person must own the full chain from training to behavior to outcome, or each team will report its own piece in isolation.

### What if we have no outcome data yet?

Report the first three levels honestly and state when outcome data will be readable, usually after one full cycle at the target stage. Show the baseline you captured so the CRO knows the comparison is coming and how it will be made.

### Should the report show individual rep results?

No. Show results by team or cohort. Individual results belong in the conversations between reps and their managers. Team-level reporting also keeps coaching coverage a shared goal rather than a ranking of managers.

### How is this different from an enablement QBR?

The monthly page tracks programs that are running and asks for small decisions. A quarterly business review steps back: which programs to continue, stop or scale, how capacity matches the sales plan and what the next quarter's priorities are.

## Sources

- [Gartner: Does your sales enablement program measure impact?](https://www.gartner.com/en/sales/trends/sales-enablement-metrics)
- [Gartner: Gartner expects sales enablement budgets to increase by 50% by 2027 (press release, February 2023)](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2023-02-15-gartner-expects-sales-enablement-budgets-to-increase-by-50-percent-by-2027)
- [Forrester: From dread to confidence, what a live experiment revealed about revenue enablement (May 2026)](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/from-dread-to-confidence-what-a-live-experiment-revealed-about-revenue-enablements-secret-powers/)
- [Kirkpatrick Partners: The Kirkpatrick Model](https://www.kirkpatrickpartners.com/the-kirkpatrick-model/)

# How to measure sales training effectiveness (and where the signal dies)

> Measure sales training effectiveness by following each skill from delivery to quota: completed, practiced, seen on real calls, then a deal stage that moved. Most reporting stops at completion because call and CRM data sit in other systems. Join training records to call evidence for one skill and one cohort, and measure at 30, 60 and 90 days.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/measuring-sales-training-effectiveness/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- Sales training reporting usually dies at step three of six, exactly where the data moves from the LMS to call recordings and the CRM.
- A 94% completion rate can hide a chain in which only five of 100 reps change behavior on real calls.
- The largest drop in most programs is from practicing once to practicing weekly, so fix that hand-off first.
- Test sales skills with realistic situations scored 0 to 100, not with knowledge quizzes.
- Measure behavior at 30, 60 and 90 days, because skills fade fast when nobody reinforces them.

Sales training is effective when reps do something differently on real calls and a deal stage moves because of it. Completion rates and survey scores cannot show that. This guide maps the Kirkpatrick Model to sales, shows the exact point where most measurement stops, and gives you a way to measure the steps that matter with the systems you already have.

## What does sales training effectiveness actually mean?

Sales training is effective when the trained behavior shows up on real calls and moves the metric at the stage where that behavior happens. Everything before that point is a precondition. Completion means the content was delivered. A quiz score means the rep recognized the right answer. Neither means the rep will say it to a CFO who has just called the price 30% too high.

The gap is large and well documented. Harvard Business Review reported that companies spent about $160 billion on employee training in the United States in 2015, and that people "soon revert to their old ways of doing things" ([HBR, 2016](https://hbr.org/2016/10/why-leadership-training-fails-and-what-to-do-about-it)). Measuring effectiveness means measuring that reversion, not the delivery.

## How does the Kirkpatrick Model map to sales training?

The Kirkpatrick Model has four levels: reaction, learning, behavior and results ([Kirkpatrick Partners](https://www.kirkpatrickpartners.com/the-kirkpatrick-model/)). They map closely to the [four levels of evidence](/guides/sales-enablement-metrics/) we use for sales enablement, with two adjustments.

| Kirkpatrick level | What it measures | Four levels of evidence | Sales-specific measure |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Reaction | Is the training relevant and engaging? | Activity | On-time completion, plus one relevance question |
| 2. Learning | Did they gain knowledge, skill, confidence? | Practice | Score on a realistic scenario, 0 to 100 |
| 3. Behavior | Do they apply it on the job? | Behavior | Share of eligible calls where the behavior appears |
| 4. Results | Did target outcomes occur? | Outcome | Conversion, discount or ramp time at the target stage |

The first adjustment: in sales, "learning" should mean demonstrated skill in a situation, not a knowledge check. The second: behavior should come from call evidence, not from surveys or self-reports. A meta-analysis of 89 transfer studies found that relationships were consistently inflated when the same source rated transfer in the same context ([Blume et al., 2010](https://doi.org/10.1177/0149206309352880)). A rep rating their own behavior is that kind of source.

Kirkpatrick Partners also advises starting with Level 4 and working backward, and starting Level 3 measurement well before 90 days so there is time to correct course. Both rules apply directly to sales programs.

## Where does the training signal die?

The training signal dies at step three of six, at the exact point where the data moves from the system enablement owns to systems it rarely touches. It does not fade gradually. It stops at a seam.

| Step | What it proves | Where the data lives |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Delivered | The rep completed the content | LMS |
| 2. Knowledge checked | The rep can recognize the right answer | LMS |
| 3. Practiced | The rep can do it in a safe setting | Roleplay or simulator tool, if anyone reads the scores |
| 4. Seen on real calls | The rep does it with buyers | Call recording or conversation intelligence |
| 5. Deal outcome | The stage moved | CRM |
| 6. Quota | Attainment changed | Finance |

Steps 1 and 2 are easy to report, so they get reported. Steps 4 to 6 require a join across systems. The fix is not another dashboard. It is one join: which reps were trained on a skill, and did the behavior appear on their calls afterward? You do not need all six steps on day one. Showing step 4 for one skill and one cohort gives you evidence no completion report can.

## Example: why 94% completion can mean five sellers changed

Example: the rates below are illustrative. They show the shape of the chain, not a benchmark. Plug in your own numbers.

| Hand-off | Reps remaining | Conversion from previous step |
|---|---|---|
| Assigned to the program | 100 | n/a |
| Completed | 94 | 94% |
| Tried the skill once in a roleplay | 60 | 64% |
| Practiced weekly | 15 | 25% |
| Had a manager ask about it in a one-to-one | 8 | 53% |
| Showed the behavior on real calls | 5 | 63% |

The dashboard is green at 94%. The number a CRO cares about is 5. Each hand-off loses people for a different, fixable reason. Practice drops because nothing asks for it. Reinforcement drops because managers are busy. On-call behavior goes unmeasured because the data sits elsewhere.

The formula is simple: **behavior yield = product of the conversion rates at each hand-off.** That makes the biggest drop the best place to act. In this example it is the step from practicing once to practicing weekly, at 25%. If a weekly practice ask from managers doubled that step to 30 reps, and the later rates held, roughly 16 reps would get reinforcement and about 10 would show the behavior on calls. One fix doubles the outcome. A better module would not.

## How do you test skill instead of knowledge?

Test skill with a realistic situation, scored, on one or two skills at a time. Knowing the answer and saying it under pressure are different abilities, and only a situation tests the second. Six rules:

1. **Keep quizzes in the LMS.** Knowledge checks are fine, but they are not a skills assessment.
2. **Build the scenario from a real deal.** The rep's industry, product and a buyer they would recognize.
3. **Test one or two skills at a time.** Ten skills in one assessment tells you nothing about any of them.
4. **Score 0 to 100.** Pass or fail hides the difference between a 71 and a 98.
5. **Show the rep the score the same day,** while the scenario is fresh.
6. **Compare cohorts, not the whole organization.** The company may be fine at negotiation while one region is not.

Name the exercise with care. "Assessment" sounds like a test of the person, and reps treat it that way. "Practice round" or "skill check" gets more honest attempts. [AI roleplay](/glossary/#ai-roleplay) makes these scenarios cheap to run at scale, and the [sales skills scorecard](/guides/sales-skills-scorecard/) shows how to report the scores.

## When should you measure, and how fast do skills fade?

Measure before training, then at 30, 60 and 90 days. Forgetting is fast without practice. A 2015 replication of Ebbinghaus' classic forgetting experiment in PLOS ONE reproduced the original curve, with most of the forgetting in the first day and only a small share retained after 31 days without relearning ([Murre and Dros, 2015](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0120644)). That study used memorized syllables, not sales skills, but the direction holds: an untouched skill decays.

Each checkpoint answers a different question:

- **Day 30:** did the behavior transfer at all?
- **Day 60:** did it survive once the launch energy was gone?
- **Day 90:** is the outcome at the target stage starting to move?

Work environment matters as much as design. The same meta-analysis found that support from the work environment was more strongly linked to transfer for open skills, such as leadership, than for closed skills, such as software use ([Blume et al., 2010](https://doi.org/10.1177/0149206309352880)). Selling is an open skill. In sales, that support is mostly the frontline manager. See [why training fades without managers](/guides/sales-manager-reinforcement/).

## What if you cannot use call data?

Many companies will not let call recordings or CRM data leave their environment, and some cannot score calls at all. Plan for that before you design the measurement.

- **Analyze where the data lives.** Run the analysis inside the company's own tools, or with a model its security team already approved. Export only a skills summary, never raw calls.
- **Treat call findings as a hypothesis.** Calls suggest a gap. A ten-minute scored scenario confirms it.
- **Look beyond calls.** Many deal-losing behaviors never appear on a recording. Was the proposal walked through live or just emailed? Were concessions traded or given away? Did the follow-up end with a dated ask? That evidence sits in email, calendars and documents. Start with three such behaviors and a human reviewer.
- **Without recordings,** use scenario scores, certifications and structured manager observations as the behavior signal, and label them as such.

Call data access is usually a legal and IT conversation before it is an analytics one. Start it in the first week, not the last.

## What to do this quarter

1. Pick one skill and one cohort. Write the behavior definition in one sentence.
2. Score a baseline of at least 30 eligible calls or scenarios before training starts.
3. Ask legal and IT for access to call data for that cohort, or agree a manager observation form.
4. Run the six-step funnel for the last program you shipped and find the biggest drop.
5. Measure behavior at 30, 60 and 90 days, and report it next to completion.

The limit: you will not get a perfect causal link from a module to a closed deal. You can get a believable chain, from training to behavior seen on calls to movement in the deals where it showed up, and that is what a CRO asks for.

If you want a second view on where your own training signal stops, the free 20-minute [Capacity Check](/#capacity-check) covers it.

## FAQ

### What are the best metrics for sales training effectiveness?

Use one metric per step of the chain: on-time completion, weekly practice rate, scenario score, behavior rate on eligible calls and the outcome at the stage the skill affects. The behavior rate is the single most useful number, because it shows transfer to real work.

### How soon after sales training should you measure results?

Take a baseline before training, then measure behavior at 30, 60 and 90 days. Thirty days shows early transfer, 60 days shows whether it survived without the launch energy, and 90 days is the earliest point most outcome metrics are worth reading.

### Is the Kirkpatrick Model still useful for sales training?

Yes, as a structure. Its four levels (reaction, learning, behavior, results) map well to sales. The adjustments for sales are to treat learning as demonstrated skill in a realistic scenario rather than a quiz score, and to measure behavior from call evidence rather than surveys.

### Why does sales training not stick?

Skills fade when reps do not practice them and managers do not ask about them. Most programs fund the event and not the weeks after it. The fix is a practice cadence, a shared scorecard and one coaching question in the existing one-to-one.

### Can you calculate the ROI of sales training?

You can estimate it, but only after you show behavior change. Multiply the outcome change at the target stage by deal value and volume, compare it with a team that started later, and subtract program cost. Without the behavior link, an ROI figure is a guess with a decimal point.

### Are post-training surveys a good measure of effectiveness?

They measure reaction, which is useful for fixing the program but weak as evidence of change. Self-reported behavior also tends to be inflated. Use surveys to check relevance and use call evidence or scored scenarios to check skill.

## Sources

- [Kirkpatrick Partners: The Kirkpatrick Model](https://www.kirkpatrickpartners.com/the-kirkpatrick-model/)
- [Murre and Dros, Replication and analysis of Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve, PLOS ONE (2015)](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0120644)
- [Blume, Ford, Baldwin and Huang, Transfer of training: a meta-analytic review, Journal of Management (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1177/0149206309352880)
- [Harvard Business Review: Why leadership training fails, and what to do about it (2016)](https://hbr.org/2016/10/why-leadership-training-fails-and-what-to-do-about-it)
