# Outsourced sales enablement: what to keep in-house and what to hand off

> Keep strategy in-house: choosing the behaviors that matter, setting priorities with the CRO, approving content and presenting results. Hand off production and operations: building assets, loading them into your tools, launching programs, chasing completion and assembling reports. A good partner works in your tools and methodology, under your approval, with a defined monthly production volume.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/outsourced-sales-enablement/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- Strategy is the scarce part of enablement; production and operations can be done by others to the enablement leader's standard.
- Keep the decide, approve and present work in-house; hand off the build, load, launch, chase and compile work.
- Marketing already works this way: an ANA survey found 82% of members run an in-house agency and 92% also use external agencies.
- Judge a partner on whether it works in your tools and methodology, reviews quality before you see it, and measures beyond completion.
- A subscription with a fixed production menu and a cap on work in progress keeps scope and cost predictable.

Outsourcing sales enablement does not mean handing your sales strategy to an outside firm. Done well, it means the reverse: your enablement leader keeps the judgment work and stops spending it on production. This guide sets out what to keep, what to hand off, how to choose a partner, which contracts work and what can go wrong.

## What is outsourced sales enablement?

Outsourced sales enablement is the use of an outside firm to do part of the enablement function's work, usually production and program operations, while the internal team keeps strategy and approval. It sits between hiring and doing nothing.

There are five common forms:

- **Sales training firms** bring their own methodology and deliver workshops.
- **Content agencies** design decks, videos and battlecards to a brief.
- **Freelancers and contractors** add hours for a specific project.
- **Fractional enablement leaders** provide part-time strategy.
- **Production and operations partners** build, launch and run programs in your tools, under your strategy.

This guide focuses on the last form, because it addresses the most common gap: the hours between a good plan and a finished, adopted program.

## Why are enablement teams handing off work?

Enablement teams hand off work because strategy is the scarce part of enablement and most of their hours go elsewhere.

Ask a head of enablement what they would do with ten more hours a week. The answers are almost always strategic: sit with front-line managers, listen to calls, rebuild onboarding around what top reps do, agree with the CRO which three behaviors matter this year. Then look at where their hours go: formatting decks, recording videos, loading modules, chasing completion, pulling reports by hand.

Headcount is not keeping up. The Sales Enablement Collective's 2025 landscape report found that 23.6% of respondents' teams shrank in headcount over the previous 12 months. Across business functions, the reasons for outsourcing have also shifted. Deloitte's 2024 Global Outsourcing Survey of more than 500 executives found that skilled talent and agility have joined cost reduction as key drivers.

Marketing solved this decades ago. A marketing leader sets strategy, and agencies and production teams build much of the output. Nobody thinks the marketing leader matters less for it. The ANA's 2023 survey of 162 marketers found that 82% of members have an in-house agency and 92% of respondents also work with external agencies. Among those using outside agencies, the average share of work done in-house is 61%. The mix is normal. The question is which work goes where.

## What should you keep in-house and what should you hand off?

Keep the work that needs your company's judgment and authority. Hand off the work that needs skill and hours but can be done to your standard by someone else.

| Work | Keep in-house | Hand off | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Enablement strategy and [charter](/glossary/#enablement-charter) | Yes | | Sets what enablement is for and what it will not do |
| Choosing three priority behaviors with the CRO | Yes | | Needs authority and access to sales leadership |
| Approving briefs, claims and final assets | Yes | | Accuracy and compliance are your accountability |
| Relationships with front-line managers | Yes | | Reinforcement depends on trust |
| Presenting results to the CRO | Yes | | The enablement leader should own the story |
| Writing, designing and recording assets | | Yes | Skilled, but repeatable to a standard |
| Building modules, roleplays and certifications in your tools | | Yes | Hours-heavy and tool-specific |
| Launching programs, nudging reps, manager lists | | Yes | Routine but time-critical |
| Platform administration | | Yes | Rarely the best use of a strategist |
| Pulling data and drafting the monthly report | | Yes | You review and present it |
| Live facilitation and kickoff production | Either | Either | Depends on your team's strengths |

The rule in short: **decide, approve and present stay in-house; build, load, launch, chase and compile can go.**

## How do you evaluate an outsourced enablement partner?

Evaluate a partner on how it fits your methodology, tools and approval process, and on what it measures. A polished portfolio matters less than these ten checks.

1. **Works in your tools.** It builds in your LMS, content platform and roleplay tool, with no proprietary platform you must adopt.
2. **Learns your methodology.** It keeps your methodology, personas, approved claims and scorecard in one reference kit and checks every asset against it.
3. **Reviews quality before you see it.** A senior reviewer approves every asset before it reaches your approver.
4. **Uses a fixed approval process.** A named approver on your side, with a set number of consolidated review rounds.
5. **Measures beyond completion.** It reports practice, behavior and outcomes, not only activity. See the [four levels of evidence](/guides/sales-enablement-metrics/).
6. **Defines volume clearly.** You know what a month buys and how many briefs can be in production at once.
7. **Stays tool-neutral.** It does not resell licenses or take vendor referral fees, so its tool advice is not paid for.
8. **Handles data and AI responsibly.** Enterprise AI agreements, no training on your data, a data protection agreement and a sub-processor list.
9. **Gives you ownership.** You own all content and data and can export it at any time.
10. **Has an exit plan.** You can see how work transfers back to your team or another partner.

Ask for sample assets built for a comparable sales motion, and a sample monthly report with names removed.

## Which contract models are common?

Five contract models are common. The right one depends on whether your need is a single project or a continuous flow of programs.

| Model | How it works | Best for | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed-fee project | One price for a defined deliverable | An onboarding rebuild, a kickoff | Change requests and no follow-up after delivery |
| Hourly or day rate | Pay for time used | Short, uncertain work | Cost is hard to predict; no incentive to be efficient |
| Retainer | Monthly fee for a block of hours | Steady, varied requests | Unused hours expire; output is not defined |
| Subscription with production menu | Monthly fee for a defined volume of assets and a cap on work in progress | Continuous program flow | Needs a clear menu and a visible usage log |
| Outcome-linked fee | Part of the fee depends on agreed results | Mature measurement | Disputes over attribution |

As one example of the subscription model, Enablement Works starts with a three-week [Diagnostic](/glossary/#enablement-diagnostic) and then runs a 12-month subscription with a fixed production menu, a cap on briefs in production at once, and a monthly report to the CRO.

## Example: what changes when production moves out

Example: a company with 400 reps has a three-person enablement team, or about 4,200 productive hours a year. Our [1:25–50 rule of thumb](/guides/sales-enablement-team-size/) puts the plan's need at 8 to 16 people. Check yours with the [enablement capacity calculator](/tools/enablement-capacity-calculator/).

Before the hand-off, the team spends about 3,000 hours on production and operations and 1,200 hours on strategy: manager work, call listening, program design and CRO reviews.

After handing off most production and operations, the team keeps about 600 hours for approvals and partner reviews. Strategy time rises from 1,200 to about 3,600 hours. The partner supplies the production hours, and the total capacity now matches more of the plan.

The point is not the total. It is that the most expensive judgment in the team is now spent on judgment.

## What are the risks, and how do you reduce them?

The main risks are generic content, loss of internal knowledge and unclear scope. Each has a specific control.

| Risk | Control |
|---|---|
| Generic, off-message content | A shared reference kit, your approval on every asset, two consolidated review rounds |
| Knowledge leaves with the partner | You keep strategy and briefs; all assets live in your tools; full export rights |
| Scope creep and surprise cost | A production menu, a work-in-progress cap and a visible usage log |
| Managers see it as an outside program | Launch under your sales leader's name and your brand |
| Tool bias | A partner that does not resell or take referral fees |
| Data exposure | A data protection agreement, zero data retention for AI, coaching scores not used in performance reviews |

## When should you not outsource sales enablement?

Do not outsource when nobody inside owns strategy, when your methodology is not yet defined, or when the team is small enough that one person can cover the work. In our experience, under about 50 reps a single enablement hire plus product marketing is usually enough. And if your content needs regulatory approval, set up the approval workflow before adding an outside producer.

## Common mistakes

- **Outsourcing strategy instead of production.** A partner cannot choose your priority behaviors for you.
- **Buying hours instead of outputs.** Define what a month delivers, not only what it costs.
- **Skipping the reference kit.** Without it, every asset becomes a rewrite.
- **Measuring the partner on volume.** Measure on programs completed and behaviors seen on calls.
- **Adding a new platform with the partner.** Use the tools you already pay for first.

To see how many enablement hours your plan needs before you decide what to hand off, the free [20-minute Capacity Check](/#capacity-check) gives you a scored estimate.

## FAQ

### Is outsourcing sales enablement the same as hiring a sales training company?

No. A sales training company usually brings its own methodology and delivers workshops. An outsourced enablement partner works in your methodology and your tools, building and running programs your team designs. Some companies use both: a training firm for the methodology and a production partner to embed it.

### How much does outsourced sales enablement cost?

Prices vary widely by model. Fixed-fee projects are priced per deliverable, such as an onboarding program. Retainers and subscriptions are priced per month for a defined production volume. Compare options on cost per adopted output, such as cost per program completed on time, rather than on monthly fee alone.

### Can a company with no enablement team outsource enablement?

It can outsource production, but someone inside must still own strategy: agreeing priorities with the CRO, approving content and acting on results. Without an internal owner, a partner ends up guessing priorities. In companies without an enablement hire, a sales leader or RevOps lead often takes this owner role.

### How long does it take an outsourced enablement partner to ramp up?

Expect two to six weeks before the first assets ship. The partner needs your methodology, personas, approved claims, brand rules and tool access. A short diagnostic at the start speeds this up, because it produces the client kit and the first program briefs together.

### Will reps know the content was built by an outside team?

They should not need to. Programs launch under your sales leader's name, in your tools, in your brand and methodology. What reps notice is whether the content is accurate and relevant, which depends on your approval process more than on who built it.

### What is a fractional head of enablement?

A fractional head of enablement is an experienced enablement leader who works part-time for several companies, usually setting strategy and building the first programs. It suits companies too small for a full-time leader. It is the opposite of a production partner: it outsources strategy rather than production.

## Sources

- [ANA: In-house agencies no longer a trend, they're here to stay (The Continued Rise of the In-House Agency, 2023 edition)](https://ana.net/content/show/id/79185)
- [Deloitte: Global Outsourcing Survey 2024](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/pages/operations/articles/global-outsourcing-survey.html)
- [Sales Enablement Collective: Sales enablement salary and landscape report 2025](https://www.salesenablementcollective.com/sales-enablement-salary-and-landscape-report/)

# Problem-first selling: what buyers still need from sellers when AI handles the information

> Problem-first selling means opening with the buyer's problem, in their words and with their number, before showing your product. When AI handles product information, buyers still need sellers for six jobs: name the problem, put a cost on it, bring one insight they lacked, build consensus, de-risk the plan, and help them justify it internally.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/problem-first-selling/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- Gartner found 61% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free buying experience, but buyers still seek seller input on whether a solution fits their situation.
- When AI covers the product facts, sellers earn their place through six jobs, all about the buyer's problem.
- The pivot from discovery to the problem statement has a fixed place: the first five minutes of call two.
- Gartner found 73% of B2B buyers actively avoid suppliers who send irrelevant outreach; default AI-written email is a fast way to become irrelevant.
- Build lookalike target lists from why customers changed, not from their firmographic profile.

A buyer can now ask an AI assistant to compare five vendors, summarize their reviews and draft questions for the demo. The product facts that sellers used to carry are a prompt away. So what do buyers still need from a seller? The answer is help with their problem, not more about your catalog. This guide sets out the six jobs that remain, shows what changes in a first meeting, and gives a worked example.

## What do buyers still need from sellers when AI handles the information?

Buyers still need sellers for judgment about their own situation: what the problem is, what it costs, and whether a solution fits. A Gartner survey of 632 B2B buyers, published in June 2025, found 61% prefer a rep-free buying experience overall. The same research found buyers prefer seller input for tasks that need contextual judgment, such as whether a product fits their company's needs. A Gartner analyst advised that sellers should offer unique guidance and act as a sounding board, rather than repeat generic information.

Buyers also arrive later and better informed. 6sense's 2025 Buyer Experience Report, based on nearly 4,000 buyers, found first contact came when buyers were about 61% through their buying process. Buyers initiated that contact 79% of the time. They bought from the vendor they ranked first 77% of the time.

Put together: the information job has moved to the buyer's own research and their AI. The decision job is still open, and that is where a seller earns a place.

## What are the six jobs of a problem-first seller?

A problem-first seller does six jobs, and every one is about the buyer's problem:

| Job | What it sounds like | What it replaces |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Name the problem | "Your stage-2 drop-off", in the buyer's words | "Pipeline challenges" |
| 2. Put a cost on it | Money per quarter, from the buyer's numbers | Generic ROI claims |
| 3. Bring one insight | One number or pattern they had not considered | A 40-slide deck |
| 4. Build consensus | A problem statement the whole group agrees with | Winning only the champion |
| 5. De-risk it | What happens if the plan is wrong, and the checkpoint | "Trust us" |
| 6. Help them justify it | A one-page case they can forward without you | A PDF proposal by email |

The job most teams skip is number 4. Sellers optimize for the champion and forget the other people who can quietly say no. Gartner found buying groups that reach consensus are 2.5 times more likely to report a high-quality deal. See [buying groups and consensus](/guides/buying-group-consensus/).

## What changes in a problem-first first meeting?

The first meeting changes from the vendor's world to the buyer's problem. Many first meetings still open with who we are, our logos, our modules and our best case study. The buyer sits through it, waiting for it to become about them. The difference shows in five places:

| Moment | Vendor-first | Problem-first |
|---|---|---|
| Slide 1 | Your logos | Their problem, stated back in their words, with their number |
| The middle | Your feature list | What the problem costs per quarter |
| Proof | Your best customer story | Evidence from their own funnel, such as where stage-2 deals stall |
| The demo | First | Only after you agree the path |
| The proposal | Emailed as a PDF | Walked through on a call where you can hear objections |

The realism line: you cannot name their number if discovery did not find one. Problem-first selling starts in call one, not on slide one.

## Where does the pivot from discovery to the problem happen?

The pivot happens in the first five minutes of call two. A common pattern among newer reps: call one goes well, with good questions and a curious buyer. Then call two opens with "let me show you the platform", and everything learned disappears into a demo. Use a fixed sequence:

1. **Call one is discovery.** No pitch. Find the problem and who owns it.
2. **Open call two with it.** "Here is what I heard last time. Tell me what I got wrong."
3. **Put a number on it.** What does this cost per quarter, in their numbers?
4. **Show the path in three steps**, not the full catalog.
5. **Confirm the sponsor.** Who signs, and do they see the problem the same way?
6. **Only then, propose.**

The moment a buyer corrects your problem statement is the most valuable minute in the deal. You learn what they care about, and they start to own the story. Some buyers want the demo first. Give it, then still state the problem back before you discuss price.

## How should AI-written follow-up change?

AI-written follow-up should carry the buyer's words and the next decision, not a default template. Gartner found 73% of B2B buyers actively avoid suppliers who send irrelevant outreach. If every seller uses the same assistant with the same default prompt, every email reads the same: a polite opening, a paragraph about the vendor, a soft ask. The buyer's own AI may summarize it as "vendor follow-up, no action needed".

Emails that get replies differ in five ways:

- The opening repeats something the buyer said, not a pleasantry.
- The ask is specific: two time slots, not "would be great to connect".
- There is one decision to make, not zero and not three.
- It is about five lines, not nine.
- It sounds like the conversation you actually had.

AI drafts are fine. The fix is the input: give the model the buyer's words, their number and the next decision. A great email cannot save a weak call. It can only carry the problem forward.

## How should targeting change?

Targeting should start from why customers changed, not from what they look like. AI agents can now take one good customer and find 20 lookalikes in minutes. But most lookalike methods copy the profile, and buyers do not buy on profile:

| Lookalike seed | What it copies | What it misses |
|---|---|---|
| Firmographics | Size, industry, region | Whether they feel the problem |
| Titles | Who signs | Who lives with the pain every day |
| Behavior signals | What they post, which tools they use | Why the last customer changed |
| Intent signals | Site visits, hiring | Whether the cost of the problem is visible yet |
| **Problem statement from the win** | **The named cost of the status quo** | Little; this is what predicts a purchase |

Start the search from "why they changed", then filter on firmographics. At the top of the funnel, profile lookalikes still beat nothing. But they fill a list, not a pipeline. If your CRM has no field for why the customer changed, add one.

## Example: a problem statement with a number

Example: in call one, a seller learns that the buyer's team creates 400 stage-2 opportunities a quarter. Conversion from stage 2 to stage 3 has fallen from 40% to 30%. Average deal size is $25,000, and about a quarter of stage-3 deals close.

The seller opens call two like this: "Last time you said stage-2 deals stall after the first demo. Conversion dropped from 40% to 30%. That is 40 fewer stage-3 deals a quarter. At your close rate and deal size, about $250,000 a quarter in bookings. Did I get that right?"

The buyer corrects one number: the close rate is closer to 20%. The cost becomes $200,000 a quarter. That correction is the point. The buyer now owns the number, and it goes on the one-page case the champion forwards to finance.

## How do you train problem-first selling?

Train it as a skill with practice, scoring and manager follow-up, not as a workshop. Three parts work well:

- **A roleplay of the call-two opening**, practiced weekly for six weeks. See [AI roleplay for sales training](/guides/ai-roleplay-sales-training/).
- **Three scored behaviors**: states the problem back, quantifies the cost, confirms who else must agree. Use one [talk track](/glossary/#talk-track) and one [skills scorecard](/guides/sales-skills-scorecard/).
- **One manager question** in each one-to-one: "What number did the buyer give you, and did they correct it?"

Start in [onboarding](/guides/sales-onboarding-program/), where habits form fastest.

## Common mistakes

- **Opening with the company story.** The buyer has read it, or asked their AI.
- **Running discovery and never saying the problem out loud.** The pivot belongs in the first five minutes of call two.
- **Using the seller's numbers instead of the buyer's.** A cost the buyer did not supply is a claim, not a problem statement.
- **Bringing ten insights.** Bring one. A number, not a deck.
- **Sending default AI-written follow-ups.** Feed the model the buyer's words and the next decision.

If you want to know whether your enablement team has the hours to build and coach this, a free [Capacity Check](/#capacity-check) takes 20 minutes.

## FAQ

### What is problem-first selling?

Problem-first selling is a sales approach that starts with the buyer's problem, stated in the buyer's words and costed with the buyer's numbers, before any product is shown. The product enters only once the buyer agrees the problem is real and worth solving.

### Do B2B buyers still want to talk to sales reps?

Less than before, and for different reasons. A Gartner survey published in June 2025 found 61% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free experience overall. But buyers still prefer seller input for judgment tasks, such as deciding whether a product fits their company's needs. That is where sellers now add value.

### How is AI changing the B2B buying process?

Buyers use AI assistants to compare vendors, summarize reviews and prepare questions before they talk to anyone. 6sense's 2025 research found buyers were about 61% through their buying process at first contact with a seller. Sellers now meet buyers who know the facts and need help with the decision.

### How do you transition from discovery to the demo?

Do not go straight from discovery to the demo. Open the next call by stating the problem back and asking the buyer what you got wrong, then put a cost on it and show a three-step path. Demo only after the buyer agrees on the problem and the path.

### What if the buyer asks for a demo first?

Give it. Some buyers want to see the product before they discuss problems. Keep it short, then still state the problem back and agree its cost before you discuss price.

### How should sellers use AI to write emails?

Use AI for drafts, but give it what only you know: the buyer's exact words, their number and the next decision. Default prompts produce emails that read like every other vendor's, which the buyer's own AI may summarize as 'no action needed'.

## Sources

- [Gartner: Gartner Sales Survey Finds 61% of B2B Buyers Prefer a Rep-Free Buying Experience (June 2025)](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-25-gartner-sales-survey-finds-61-percent-of-b2b-buyers-prefer-a-rep-free-buying-experience)
- [CustomerThink: 6sense Study Provides Critical Insights on B2B Buyer Behavior (2025 Buyer Experience Report)](https://customerthink.com/research-round-up-6sense-study-provides-critical-insights-on-b2b-buyer-behavior/)
- [Gartner: Gartner Sales Survey Finds 74% of B2B Buyer Teams Demonstrate Unhealthy Conflict During the Decision Process (May 2025)](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process)

# Coaching coverage: the sales coaching metric most teams can't answer

> Coaching coverage is the share of reps who had at least one documented coaching conversation with their manager in the last 30 days, based on a real call or a scored roleplay. Formula: reps coached ÷ active reps × 100. Our rule of thumb: below 50% is a gap, 70–85% is healthy, and above 90% deserves a quality check.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/sales-coaching-coverage/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- Coaching coverage is the share of reps who had at least one documented, evidence-based coaching conversation with their manager in the last 30 days.
- Most sales organizations cannot report coaching coverage because nobody records coaching in a consistent way.
- Our rule of thumb: below 50% coverage is a gap, 70–85% is healthy, and above 90% should trigger a check of quality.
- Three changes make coverage measurable and higher: one shared three-behavior scorecard, a weekly note to each manager, and coverage reported by team.
- Coverage measures reach, not quality, so pair it with follow-through and call evidence.

Ask a CRO one question: in the last 30 days, what share of your reps had at least one documented coaching conversation with their manager, based on a real call or a roleplay? Most cannot answer it. That number is coaching coverage, and it tells you more about whether enablement will stick than any completion rate. This guide defines it, gives the formula and target ranges, and shows the three changes that make it measurable and higher.

## What is coaching coverage?

Coaching coverage is the percentage of active reps who had at least one documented, evidence-based coaching conversation with their manager in the last 30 days. Programs teach. Managers make it stick. Coverage is the simplest measure of whether the second part is happening at all.

A conversation counts only if it meets four tests:

1. **One rep.** It is a one-to-one, not a team meeting.
2. **Evidence.** It uses a recorded call, a live call the manager joined, or a scored roleplay.
3. **One behavior.** It names a specific behavior, ideally one from the team's shared scorecard.
4. **A next step.** It ends with a drill or a thing to try on the next call, and it is written down.

Pipeline reviews, forecast calls and deal inspections do not count. They matter, but they coach the deal, not the rep's skill. See the [glossary entry for coaching coverage](/glossary/#coaching-coverage).

## How do you calculate coaching coverage?

Use this formula:

**Coaching coverage = reps with at least one documented coaching conversation in the last 30 days ÷ active reps × 100**

"Active reps" means quota-carrying reps who worked for most of the 30 days. Exclude reps on leave. Include new hires from their third week. Use a rolling 30-day window, not a calendar month, so the number does not jump at month end.

Coverage alone measures reach. Three companion metrics tell you about depth and quality:

| Metric | Formula | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| Coaching coverage | Reps coached in 30 days ÷ active reps | Reach: is anyone left out? |
| Coaching depth | Coaching conversations ÷ reps coached | Frequency for those who are coached |
| Coaching focus | Conversations on the quarter's priority skill ÷ all conversations | Alignment with the enablement plan |
| Follow-through | Coached reps re-observed on the same behavior within 30 days ÷ reps coached | Whether coaching closes the loop |

Start with coverage. Add the other three once the logging habit exists.

## What is a good coaching coverage rate?

As our rule of thumb, 70–85% coverage in a 30-day window is healthy for a sales team. Below 50%, many reps get no skill coaching at all. Above 90% is possible but rare, and it should prompt a check that the logged conversations are real. These ranges are our working benchmarks, not published industry figures.

| Coverage | What it usually means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Below 30% | Coaching is left to each manager's habits | Introduce the scorecard and the logging step |
| 30–50% | A few managers coach; most do not | Send the weekly manager note; report by team |
| 50–70% | The habit is forming | Add the focus and follow-through metrics |
| 70–85% | Healthy | Shift attention to quality and call evidence |
| Above 90% | Excellent, or inflated | Sample ten logged conversations and check the evidence |

Why not aim for 100%? Holidays, new managers and wide spans of control make it unrealistic. The time math also matters. A manager with ten reps who holds one 30-minute evidence-based conversation per rep each month, plus 15 minutes of preparation, spends about 7.5 hours a month. That is less than two hours a week. With 15 reps, it is almost three hours a week, and coverage drops first.

## Why does coaching coverage matter more than completion rates?

Completion tells you a program was delivered. Coverage tells you whether anyone is helping reps apply it on real deals, and survey research ties structured coaching to better results.

The CSO Insights 2019 Sales Enablement Report, based on more than 900 participants, found that 62.9% of organizations left coaching to managers or followed informal guidelines. Only 37.1% had a formal or dynamic approach. Organizations with dynamic coaching, meaning formal coaching aligned to the enablement services reps received, reported a 55.2% win rate. Where coaching was left to managers, the win rate was 41.8%. The study average was 46.4%.

Korn Ferry reports a similar gap. Its research cites a 28% increase in quota attainment and a 32% increase in win rates from effective sales coaching, and a Korn Ferry poll found that 80% of sales leaders had no formal, or an inconsistent, coaching process. Earlier, Matthew Dixon and Brent Adamson wrote in Harvard Business Review (2011) that research by the Sales Executive Council found no other productivity investment close to coaching for improving rep performance.

The constraint is time and insight, not belief. Gartner's 2025 research on data-driven coaching says sales managers know coaching drives performance but lack either the insights or the time to coach well. Coverage makes that constraint visible.

The limit: these are correlations from surveys. Organizations that coach well may also hire, pay and manage well. Coverage is a leading indicator, not a guarantee.

## Why can't most sales teams answer the coverage question?

Most teams cannot report coverage because nobody records coaching consistently. Managers coach when they can, on what they notice, to their own standard. Some write notes in a document, some in the CRM, most nowhere. Without a shared definition and a 60-second logging step, the honest answer to "what is our coverage?" is "we don't know".

## The three changes that make coverage measurable and higher

Three changes do most of the work. None of them needs a new tool.

1. **A short scorecard of three behaviors.** Pick the three behaviors that matter most this quarter and use them everywhere: in content, in roleplays and in manager coaching. When the rep, the roleplay and the manager grade the same three things, coaching gets faster and logging gets easier. The [sales skills scorecard](/guides/sales-skills-scorecard/) guide shows how to build one.
2. **A weekly note to each manager.** Every Monday, send each manager one short note per rep: one strength, one gap and one drill, drawn from roleplay scores and recent calls. The manager starts from a draft instead of a blank page. A draft gets used; a blank page gets postponed.
3. **Coverage reported by team, not by manager.** Put coverage on the monthly [CRO report](/guides/enablement-report-for-cro/) as a team number. That makes it a shared goal for the sales leader rather than a ranking of managers. Share manager-level data privately.

To record it, create a coaching activity in your CRM or coaching tool with four fields: rep, evidence link, behavior and next drill. If logging takes more than a minute, managers will stop.

## Five coaching complaints and their usual causes

The symptom a team reports is usually two steps away from the cause, and the fix is rarely more content.

| Complaint | Usual instinct | Usual cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Reps don't log in to practice." | Send reminders, change the tool | Their manager never asks about it | Manager reads scores weekly and mentions them |
| "Scores plateau." | Make scenarios harder | Scenarios do not feel like the rep's world | Build the scenario from the rep's own open deal |
| "We're bad at negotiation." | Train everyone | One cohort is struggling | Score by cohort and coach that cohort |
| "Great feedback, no change." | Better feedback | No follow-through on a live deal | Manager coaches one real deal per rep using the skill |
| "They did the simulation once." | Blame motivation | No frequency rule | Weekly practice, scored |

Sometimes the product really is the problem. Check the manager first, because it is cheaper.

## Example: raising coverage from 38% to 78% in a quarter

Example: a sales team has 120 reps and 12 managers. In the first month of logging, 46 reps have a documented, evidence-based coaching conversation. Coverage is 46 ÷ 120 = 38%. One team is at 10%; another is at 80%.

The team introduces a three-behavior scorecard, a Monday manager note and team-level reporting. By month three, two reps are on leave, so 118 reps are active. 92 have a documented conversation. Coverage is 92 ÷ 118 = 78%. Depth is 1.4 conversations per coached rep, and 70% of conversations are on the quarter's priority skill. The 10% team is now at 55%, and its second-line manager gets a private view of which reps are still uncoached.

## Common mistakes

- **Counting pipeline reviews as coaching.** They coach the deal, not the behavior.
- **Ranking managers in public.** It produces logging, not coaching.
- **Logging without evidence.** A note that says "discussed discovery" with no call or roleplay attached is not coaching.
- **Coaching everything at once.** A conversation that covers five skills teaches none. Keep it to one behavior from the scorecard.

## What are the limits of coaching coverage?

Coverage measures reach, not quality. A manager can hit 100% with weak conversations. That is why follow-through and call evidence matter: they show whether the coached behavior appears on the next calls. Coverage also depends on honest logging, so sample a few conversations each month. For the bigger picture of what managers must do beyond coaching, read [why sales training fades without managers](/guides/sales-manager-reinforcement/).

If you want to know your coaching coverage and the hours it would take to raise it, start with a free [20-minute Capacity Check](/#capacity-check).

## FAQ

### How often should sales managers coach each rep?

At least one documented, evidence-based coaching conversation per rep every 30 days is the floor. Many teams aim for two a month for reps in their first year. Frequency matters less than whether each conversation uses a real call or roleplay and ends with one drill.

### What counts as a coaching conversation?

A one-to-one conversation that uses evidence (a recorded call, a live call the manager joined, or a scored roleplay), names one behavior and ends with a specific next step. Pipeline reviews, forecast calls and team meetings do not count.

### How do you track sales coaching in a CRM?

Create a coaching activity type with four fields: rep, evidence link, behavior coached and next drill. Logging takes under a minute. Coverage then becomes a simple report of distinct reps with a coaching activity in the last 30 days.

### What is a good coaching coverage rate?

As our rule of thumb, 70–85% of active reps in a 30-day window is healthy. Below 50% means many reps are not coached at all. Above 90% is possible, but check that the logged conversations are real and evidence-based.

### Does sales coaching improve win rates?

Survey research points that way. The CSO Insights 2019 Sales Enablement Report found a 55.2% win rate for organizations with a dynamic coaching approach, against 41.8% where coaching was left to managers. That is a correlation, not proof of cause, but it is consistent across years of that study.

### Should coaching coverage be reported by manager?

Report it by team first. Ranking managers publicly turns coverage into a compliance number and invites fake logging. Share manager-level data privately with each manager and their leader.

## Sources

- [CSO Insights (Miller Heiman Group): 2019 Sales Enablement Report](https://community.highspot.com/assets/2019/10/CSO-Insights-5th-Annual-Sales-Enablement-Study.pdf)
- [Korn Ferry: Seize the Sale, create impact through sales coaching](https://www.kornferry.com/about-us/events-webinars/seize-the-sale-create-impact-through-sales-coaching)
- [Harvard Business Review: Dixon and Adamson, The Dirty Secret of Effective Sales Coaching (2011)](https://hbr.org/2011/01/the-dirty-secret-of-effective)
- [Gartner: Equip Managers With Data-Driven Coaching to Boost Seller Performance (2025)](https://www.gartner.com/en/documents/6928866)

# Sales enablement metrics: the four levels of evidence a CRO will fund

> Measure sales enablement at four levels of evidence: activity (did reps complete it?), practice (can they do it in a roleplay?), behavior (do they do it on real calls?) and outcome (did ramp time, stage conversion or win rate move?). Set the baseline before launch and start one team 30 days before another, so you have a comparison.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/sales-enablement-metrics/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- Sales enablement metrics fall into four levels of evidence: activity, practice, behavior and outcome, and a CRO funds only plans that reach levels 3 and 4.
- Measure behavior as a share of eligible calls, the calls where the moment actually arose, not as a share of all calls.
- Pick the outcome metric at the stage the behavior should move, not whole-funnel conversion or total revenue.
- Set every baseline before launch; a baseline taken after launch is already contaminated by the program.
- Starting one team 30 days before another gives you a comparison group at no extra cost.

Most enablement dashboards report what is easy to count: completions, logins and content views. Those numbers prove that work was delivered. They do not prove that anything changed in the field, and a CRO funds change. This guide sets out the four levels of evidence, the formulas for each, and a simple way to build a comparison that a skeptical finance partner will accept.

## What are the four levels of evidence?

The four levels of evidence are activity, practice, behavior and outcome. Each level answers a different question, uses data from a different system and has a different owner. A report that stops at level 1 describes effort. A report that reaches level 4 describes impact.

| Level | Question it answers | Example metrics | Where the data lives | Usual owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Activity | Did reps complete the program? | On-time completion, time to start, active users | LMS, content platform | Enablement |
| 2. Practice | Can they do it when asked? | Roleplay scores, certification pass rate, practice frequency | Roleplay tool, certification records | Enablement |
| 3. Behavior | Do they do it on real calls? | Behavior rate on eligible calls, coaching coverage | Call recordings, manager observations | Frontline managers |
| 4. Outcome | Did a business number move? | Ramp time, conversion at the target stage, win rate, discount depth | CRM, finance | Sales leadership |

Level 3 depends on recorded calls. Where calls are not recorded, use roleplay scores, certifications and structured manager observations as the behavior signal, and say so on the report. The [glossary entry](/glossary/#four-levels-of-evidence) has a one-line definition you can reuse.

The levels follow the logic of the Kirkpatrick Model, which also moves from learning to on-the-job behavior to results. Kirkpatrick Partners advises starting with the results level and working backward ([Kirkpatrick Partners](https://www.kirkpatrickpartners.com/the-kirkpatrick-model/)). That is the right order for planning, too: agree the outcome first, then the behavior that drives it, then the practice and the activity.

## Why don't activity metrics get funded?

Activity metrics do not get funded because they measure what enablement produced, not what the field changed. A CRO plans against quota. A 94% completion rate says nothing about whether more sellers will reach it.

The opposite mistake is just as common. Gartner's research on [sales enablement metrics](https://www.gartner.com/en/sales/trends/sales-enablement-metrics) found that more than two-thirds of enablement leaders measure their impact by pipeline conversion rates, a number enablement has little direct effect on. Overall conversion depends on pricing, product, competition and lead quality. Claiming it invites a fair challenge, and losing that challenge costs credibility.

The four levels sit between those two errors. They connect what enablement controls (levels 1 and 2) to what managers control (level 3), then to one business number the behavior should move (level 4). The discipline pays: Forrester's 2025 B2B Sales Survey found that high-performing sales teams were 37% more likely to measure the impact of enablement on the wider organization ([Forrester, 2026](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/from-dread-to-confidence-what-a-live-experiment-revealed-about-revenue-enablements-secret-powers/)).

## Which metrics belong at each level?

Use two or three metrics per level and write down the formula for each, so anyone in RevOps can rerun it.

### Level 1: Activity

- **On-time completion rate** = reps who completed by the due date ÷ reps assigned.
- **Time to start** = median days from launch to first module opened. A long time to start usually means managers did not mention the program.
- **Cost per active user** = annual license cost ÷ reps active in the last 30 days. Run it for every tool with the [cost per active user calculator](/tools/cost-per-active-user-calculator/).

### Level 2: Practice

- **Weekly practice rate** = reps with at least one scored roleplay in the week ÷ reps assigned. One attempt in launch week is curiosity. Weekly attempts are practice.
- **Skill score** = median 0–100 score per skill, by team.
- **Share at benchmark** = reps scoring 70 or above ÷ reps scored. The line at 70 is our working benchmark; the [sales skills scorecard guide](/guides/sales-skills-scorecard/) explains how to set it.

### Level 3: Behavior

- **Behavior rate** = calls where the target behavior appears ÷ eligible calls. An eligible call is one where the moment arose: a price objection, a new stakeholder, a first discovery call. Dividing by all calls understates rare behaviors and hides real change.
- **Coaching coverage** = reps with at least one documented coaching conversation, based on a real call or a roleplay, in the last 30 days ÷ all reps. See [coaching coverage](/guides/sales-coaching-coverage/) for how to record it.

### Level 4: Outcome

Choose the outcome the behavior should move, at the stage where the behavior happens. A discovery program should move conversion from discovery to the next stage. A negotiation program should move discount depth or late-stage win rate. A new-hire program should move ramp time, defined as days from start date to a set share of quota.

Avoid whole-funnel numbers and total revenue unless the program truly covers the whole funnel. They are too far from the behavior and too exposed to other causes.

## How do you set a baseline before the program starts?

Measure every metric you plan to report before launch, using the same definitions you will use afterward. Gartner makes the same point: leaders "must first establish a baseline for the targeted behaviors" before they can show enablement impact ([Gartner, 2023](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2023-02-15-gartner-expects-sales-enablement-budgets-to-increase-by-50-percent-by-2027)).

A practical baseline takes about two weeks:

1. Score a sample of at least 30 eligible calls per team on the target behavior, from the six weeks before launch.
2. Pull the last two quarters of the outcome metric for each team, so you can see normal variation.
3. Record current practice and certification levels, even if they are zero.
4. Write the metric definitions on one page and freeze them for the life of the program.

A baseline taken after launch is already contaminated. Early adopters change first, and the "before" number drifts upward.

## How does a 30-day staggered start create a comparison?

Start one team 30 days before a similar team. For those 30 days, the later team is your comparison group: same quarter, same pricing, same comp plan, same market. The only planned difference is the program. Then the later team starts, so nobody misses out.

The formula is a difference-in-differences:

**Program effect = (early team after − early team before) − (later team after − later team before)**

Three rules keep the comparison fair. Pick teams of similar size, segment and tenure. Do not give the early slot to the strongest manager. Where you can, decide the order by coin flip and write down that you did.

## Example: one program, four levels, two teams

Example: a company runs a discovery program for two teams of 40 reps each. Team A starts on 1 October. Team B starts on 1 November. The table shows the position on 31 October.

| Metric | Team A before | Team A day 30 | Team B before | Team B day 30 | Program effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| On-time completion | 0% | 90% | 0% | 0% | n/a |
| Weekly practice rate | 0% | 45% | 0% | 0% | n/a |
| Behavior rate on eligible calls | 22% | 41% | 24% | 25% | +18 points |
| Discovery-to-next-stage conversion | 31% | 36% | 30% | 31% | +4 points |

Behavior rose 19 points in Team A and 1 point in Team B, so the program effect is 18 points. Conversion rose 5 points against 1, so the effect is 4 points.

Now the honest reading. Behavior moved clearly. Conversion moved in the same direction, but with about 150 discovery opportunities per team per month, a 4-point gap is within normal monthly noise. The report should say: "Behavior changed. Conversion is moving the right way. We will confirm over the quarter." That sentence is believable, and a believable chain gets funded.

## Who owns the chain from training to quota?

Training sits with enablement, behavior sits with frontline managers and quota sits with sales leadership. In most companies nobody owns the hand-off between them, so each level gets reported alone and nobody draws the line from one to the next.

The signal usually dies where the data changes systems: from the LMS, which enablement owns, to call recordings and the CRM, which it rarely touches. The fix is one join: which reps were trained on a skill, and did the behavior show up on their calls afterward? Call data access is often a legal and IT conversation before it is an analytics one, so start it early. [Measuring sales training effectiveness](/guides/measuring-sales-training-effectiveness/) walks through that seam in detail, and the [one-page CRO report](/guides/enablement-report-for-cro/) shows where each level lands each month.

## Common mistakes

- **Reporting completion as success.** Completion is the price of entry. Report it, but never as the headline.
- **Claiming whole-funnel numbers.** Total pipeline conversion or revenue invites challenges you cannot win.
- **Setting the baseline after launch.** The "before" number is already moving by then.
- **Dividing by all calls.** Use eligible calls, or rare behaviors will look absent.
- **Changing definitions mid-program.** A new formula in month two breaks every trend line.

The limit: no metric set gives a perfect causal link from a module to a closed deal. What it gives you is a chain a CRO can follow, from practice to behavior to a stage that moved, with a comparison group beside it.

If you want to see which of the four levels your current reporting reaches, the free 20-minute [Capacity Check](/#capacity-check) is a quick place to start.

## FAQ

### What are the most important sales enablement KPIs?

Pick one or two per level: on-time completion (activity), weekly practice rate and share of reps at benchmark (practice), behavior rate on eligible calls and coaching coverage (behavior), and the outcome at the stage the program targets (outcome). Eight metrics on one page is enough for most programs.

### Should sales enablement be measured on win rate?

Only when the program targets the late stages of a deal, such as negotiation or the final proposal. For discovery or prospecting programs, win rate is too far from the behavior and too exposed to pricing, product and competition. Use conversion at the stage the behavior happens instead.

### How long before sales enablement metrics show results?

Activity and practice move within two weeks of launch. Behavior on calls usually shows by day 30 if managers reinforce the program. Outcome metrics need at least one full sales cycle at the target stage, often 60 to 120 days, before the numbers are worth reading.

### What is a leading indicator for sales enablement?

Practice frequency and behavior rate on eligible calls are the most useful leading indicators. They move weeks before outcomes and they are close enough to the program that enablement and managers can act on them. Completion is a precondition, not a leading indicator.

### Can you measure sales enablement without a control group?

Yes, but the claim is weaker. Compare each team to its own baseline and look for a dose effect: reps who practiced more should show the behavior more. A staggered start is better and costs almost nothing, because every team still gets the program.

### How many metrics should a sales enablement dashboard have?

Two or three per level, so eight to twelve in total. More than that and nobody reads past the first screen. Every metric should have a written formula and a named owner.

## Sources

- [Gartner: Gartner expects sales enablement budgets to increase by 50% by 2027 (press release, February 2023)](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2023-02-15-gartner-expects-sales-enablement-budgets-to-increase-by-50-percent-by-2027)
- [Forrester: From dread to confidence, what a live experiment revealed about revenue enablement (May 2026)](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/from-dread-to-confidence-what-a-live-experiment-revealed-about-revenue-enablements-secret-powers/)
- [Kirkpatrick Partners: The Kirkpatrick Model](https://www.kirkpatrickpartners.com/the-kirkpatrick-model/)

# How to build a 12-month sales enablement roadmap

> A 12-month sales enablement roadmap starts with capacity, not ideas. Size the hours your sales plan needs against the hours your team has. Agree three priority behaviors with the CRO. Place fixed work such as onboarding, launches and the kickoff first, then sequence skill programs into quarters with baselines set beforehand. Review results and re-plan every quarter.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/sales-enablement-roadmap/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- Build the roadmap in six steps: diagnose capacity, place fixed work, agree three behaviors, sequence programs, set baselines, review every quarter.
- Compare the hours the plan needs with the hours the team has before choosing any program; the gap decides what you cut, defer or hand off.
- Three priority behaviors, agreed with the CRO and tied to a stage metric, are enough for one year.
- Every program on the roadmap should carry its own reinforcement: practice, a manager ask and checks at day 30, 60 and 90.
- Keep about 15% of hours in reserve, because sales organizations change direction several times a year.

Most enablement roadmaps are lists of good ideas with dates attached. They fail in the same way: the ideas outnumber the hours, the follow-up is cut first, and by the third quarter the plan is a record of what slipped. This guide builds the roadmap the other way round, starting from capacity and three agreed behaviors.

## What is a sales enablement roadmap?

A sales enablement roadmap is a 12-month plan that sets which programs enablement will run, in which order, for whom, with how many hours, and how each will be measured. It is agreed with the CRO and reviewed every quarter.

It is not a content calendar. A content calendar lists assets. A roadmap lists programs, and a program includes the asset plus the launch, the practice, the manager reinforcement and the measurement.

## Step 1: How do you diagnose enablement capacity?

Start by comparing the hours your sales plan needs from enablement with the hours your team has. This one comparison decides everything that follows.

A good diagnosis covers five things:

1. **Capacity.** List next year's hires, launches, kickoff and programs. Estimate hours for each and compare with your team's productive hours (about 1,400 per person a year is our planning assumption). The [enablement capacity calculator](/tools/enablement-capacity-calculator/) does this for you.
2. **Tools.** Calculate the [cost per active user](/guides/cost-per-active-user/) of each enablement tool. Half-used tools often signal missing operations hours, not a bad tool.
3. **Content.** Find your 20 most-used assets and check their age and accuracy.
4. **Behavior.** Listen to calls, or read roleplay scores, and note which behaviors separate top reps from the rest.
5. **Stakeholders.** Interview the CRO, five to ten managers and a few top reps about what they need.

If the gap between hours needed and hours available is large, the roadmap must cut, defer or hand off work. Pretending otherwise produces a plan that fails by spring. The [team size guide](/guides/sales-enablement-team-size/) explains the 1:25–50 rule of thumb behind this check.

## Step 2: What work is already fixed?

Some enablement work is not optional, because the sales plan already commits you to it. Place it on the roadmap first.

- **Onboarding cohorts.** Every planned hire needs a ramp program. The Bridge Group's 2026 AE report, covering 158 B2B companies, found average AE ramp time of 6.2 months, the highest in the study's history. Each cohort needs support for most of that time.
- **Product launches.** Their dates come from product and marketing.
- **The sales kickoff and its 90 days.** The event is the easy part. The certification, roleplays, manager lists and day-30, 60 and 90 reports are where the money pays off. See [the 90-day plan after a kickoff](/guides/sales-kickoff-follow-up/).
- **Compliance and annual certifications,** where your industry requires them.

Then set aside a reserve. Gartner's 2026 survey of 227 chief sales officers found that sales organizations completed an average of four transformations in the previous 12 months. Something will change mid-year. Our rule of thumb is to hold about 15% of hours in reserve for it.

## Step 3: How do you choose three behaviors with the CRO?

Agree three seller behaviors that matter most this year, each observable on calls and tied to a sales stage metric. Three is enough. More than three spreads practice and manager attention too thin to change anything.

Use evidence, not opinion: call reviews, win-loss notes, stage conversion data and what top reps do differently. A good behavior passes four tests:

1. **Observable.** A manager can see or hear it on a call or in a roleplay.
2. **Scorable.** It fits on a short scorecard with clear criteria.
3. **Linked.** It connects to one stage metric.
4. **Coachable.** A manager can coach it in a weekly one-to-one.

| Behavior | Seen on calls as | Linked metric |
|---|---|---|
| Quantify the buyer's problem | Rep records a cost or metric of the problem by the second call | Stage 1 to stage 2 conversion |
| Reach the buying group | Three or more engaged contacts before a proposal | Win rate on proposals |
| Hold price with value | Rep ties price to the quantified problem before discussing discount | Average discount |

Write the three behaviors down and get the CRO to sign them. This matters more than it sounds. The Sales Enablement Collective's 2025 landscape report found that only 43.8% of respondents are aligned with their senior leadership on metrics. A signed list of three behaviors and their metrics closes most of that gap.

## Step 4: How do you sequence programs across the year?

Sequence programs so the fixed work lands first, one behavior is trained at a time, and every program includes its own reinforcement. Six rules keep the sequence realistic:

1. **Fixed work first.** Onboarding, launches and the kickoff go on the calendar before anything else.
2. **One behavior per [skill sprint](/glossary/#skill-sprint).** Train one behavior for about six weeks, with scored practice and manager coaching, then move to the next.
3. **Reinforcement is part of the program.** Memory research has shown for over a century that new material fades fast without review. Murre and Dros's 2015 replication of Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, published in PLOS ONE, reproduced the classic shape: steep loss soon after learning, then a slower decline. So no program launches without practice, a manager ask and checks at day 30, 60 and 90.
4. **Cap work in progress.** For a team of three, run no more than three major programs at once.
5. **Stagger starts where you can.** Start one team 30 days before another, so you can compare them.
6. **Protect the reserve.** Do not spend it in the first quarter.

## Step 5: How do you set baselines and measures?

Set the baseline for each program before it starts, using four levels of evidence: activity, practice, behavior and outcome. A baseline set after a program cannot show change.

For each program, record the current completion norm, the current practice score, how often the behavior appears on calls today (or in roleplays and manager observations, where calls are not recorded), and the linked stage metric for the last two quarters. The [sales enablement metrics guide](/guides/sales-enablement-metrics/) covers each level.

## Step 6: How do you run the quarterly review?

Hold a 60-minute review with the CRO every quarter, and re-plan the next quarter in detail. A fixed agenda keeps it short:

1. What shipped against plan, and what slipped.
2. Results by program, at each of the four levels.
3. Hours used against plan, and the reserve remaining.
4. Tool usage and cost per active user.
5. What to stop.
6. Next quarter's programs and any change to the three behaviors.

Invite product marketing and customer success leaders. Gartner's 2026 CSO survey found that sales organizations that create enablement content together with marketing and service are 2.4 times more likely to achieve strong commercial growth.

## Example: a roadmap for a 250-rep team

Example: a company has 250 reps and 25 managers. The plan includes 70 new hires, three launches, a January kickoff and three skill sprints. The enablement team has three people, or 4,200 hours.

Using our planning assumptions, the plan needs 8,200 hours: onboarding 2,100, launches 900, kickoff and follow-up 1,000, skill sprints 900, coaching support 1,800, and content, tools and reporting 1,500. A 15% reserve adds about 1,200, for 9,400 in total. The gap is 5,200 hours.

The CRO makes four decisions. Drop the third skill sprint (saves 300 hours). Hire one person in the second quarter (adds about 1,000 hours this year). Hand off production work worth 3,500 hours. Reduce the reserve to 800 hours. Need and capacity now both come to 8,700 hours.

| Quarter | Programs | Measures |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Kickoff plus 90-day follow-up; onboarding rebuild; baselines for behaviors 1 and 2 | Certification rate by week 2; day-30, 60 and 90 reports |
| Q2 | Skill sprint 1: quantify the problem; launch A; new hire joins | Practice scores; behavior on calls; stage 1 to 2 conversion |
| Q3 | Skill sprint 2: reach the buying group; launch B; tool review | Engaged contacts per proposal; cost per active user |
| Q4 | Launch C; next year's capacity model and kickoff design | Win rate on proposals; ramp time for Q2 cohort |

## What to do this quarter

1. Run the capacity comparison: hours needed against hours available.
2. Place onboarding, launches and the kickoff on a 12-month calendar.
3. Draft three behaviors with evidence, and get the CRO to sign them.
4. Decide with the CRO how to close the hours gap: cut, defer, hire or hand off.
5. Set baselines for the first two programs.
6. Book the four quarterly reviews now.

If you want an outside view of step 1, the free [20-minute Capacity Check](/#capacity-check) gives you a scored capacity estimate the next day.

## FAQ

### What should a sales enablement roadmap include?

It should include the three priority behaviors, each program with its owner, start date and audience, the hours each program needs, the measure and baseline for each program, and the review dates. It should also list what enablement will not do this year, so requests outside the plan have a clear answer.

### Who should approve the sales enablement roadmap?

The CRO or head of sales should approve it, because they control manager time and own the outcomes. Product marketing, RevOps and customer success leaders should review it before approval, since launches, data and post-sale hand-offs depend on them.

### How do you handle requests that are not on the roadmap?

Compare each request with the three priority behaviors and the reserve hours. If it supports a priority and the reserve has room, take it. If it does not, log it for the quarterly review. A written list of what is out of scope makes these conversations shorter.

### How is a roadmap different from an enablement charter?

A charter defines what enablement is for, who it serves, what it owns and how success is measured. It changes rarely. A roadmap applies the charter to one year: which programs, in which order, with which hours. Write the charter first, then the roadmap.

### What should a new head of enablement do in the first 90 days?

Spend the first month on diagnosis: interview the CRO, managers and top reps, audit tools and content, and listen to calls. Spend the second month agreeing three behaviors and a capacity model. Use the third month to ship one visible program, often onboarding or kickoff follow-up, while drafting the full roadmap.

### How often should you update a sales enablement roadmap?

Review it every quarter with the CRO and re-plan the next quarter in detail. Keep later quarters at a lower level of detail, since launches and priorities will shift. Change the three priority behaviors only when evidence shows one is solved or no longer matters.

## Sources

- [Gartner: Gartner predicts AI-driven sales enablement will deliver 40% faster sales stage velocity than traditional enablement methods by 2029 (April 2026)](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-04-01-gartner-predicts-ai-driven-sales-enablement-will-deliver-40-percent-faster-sales-stage-velocity-than-traditional-enablement-methods-by-20291)
- [Sales Enablement Collective: Sales enablement salary and landscape report 2025](https://www.salesenablementcollective.com/sales-enablement-salary-and-landscape-report/)
- [The Bridge Group: 2026 AE models, motions and metrics](https://www.bridgegroupinc.com/research/2026-ae-models-motions-metrics)
- [PLOS ONE: Murre and Dros, Replication and analysis of Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve (2015)](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0120644)

# Sales enablement ROI: how to measure enablement output per dollar

> Measure sales enablement ROI in two steps. First, calculate enablement output per dollar: total annual enablement spend set against the outputs that reached the field and were used, such as programs completed on time, reps certified and behaviors seen on calls. Second, link one program to one business outcome, such as ramp time, against a baseline set beforehand.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/sales-enablement-roi/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- Enablement output per dollar = adopted outputs ÷ total annual enablement spend, where outputs are programs completed on time, reps certified, reps practicing and behaviors seen on calls.
- Most enablement money leaks in three places: platforms paid for and half-used, programs built and never followed up, and skilled people spending their week on production.
- Classic training ROI is (net program benefits ÷ program costs) × 100, and it only works for one program measured against a baseline or a comparison group.
- AI made assets cheap, but the asset was never the expensive part, so output per dollar rises only when saved hours go into operations and measurement.

Sales leaders track cost per lead, cost per meeting and cost per closed deal. Almost nobody tracks what each enablement dollar produces. This guide gives you a formula you can run this quarter, the three places the money usually leaks, and an honest way to link one program to revenue.

## Why is sales enablement ROI hard to measure?

Sales enablement ROI is hard to measure because revenue has many causes and enablement is only one of them. Pricing, territory changes, hiring, product releases and the market all move at the same time as your program.

The classic training formula, from the Phillips ROI methodology summarized by Training Industry, is:

**ROI (%) = (net program benefits ÷ program costs) × 100**

The formula is simple. The hard part is the step before it: isolating how much of the benefit came from the program and converting it to money. That is possible for one well-designed program. It is not practical for a whole enablement budget every quarter.

So we split the question in two:

1. **Efficiency:** what did the enablement budget produce that reached the field and was used? That is [enablement output per dollar](/glossary/#enablement-output-per-dollar).
2. **Effect:** for one program at a time, did a business outcome move against a baseline? That is classic ROI.

## What is enablement output per dollar?

Enablement output per dollar is the number of adopted outputs that reached the field, divided by total annual enablement spend. In practice it is easier to read as its inverse: cost per adopted output.

**Total spend** includes everything: fully loaded enablement salaries, platform licenses, content and video production, external partners, and the enablement share of the kickoff.

**Adopted outputs** count only what reached reps and was used. A course that was built but not completed does not count. A battlecard that nobody opened does not count.

| Unit metric | Formula | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| Cost per program completed on time | Total spend ÷ programs that hit their completion target by the deadline | Whether the team finishes what it starts |
| Cost per certified rep | Total spend ÷ reps who passed a certification | How much it costs to get a rep to a tested standard |
| Cost per practicing rep | Total spend ÷ reps practicing at least twice a month | Whether practice became a habit |
| Cost per rep showing the behavior | Total spend ÷ reps whose calls or roleplays show the target behavior | The closest efficiency measure to revenue |
| [Cost per active user](/guides/cost-per-active-user/) | Annual license cost ÷ reps active in the last 30 days | Whether each tool earns its renewal |

Pick two or three of these, not all five. Report them every quarter. The trend matters more than the first number.

## Where does enablement money leak?

Enablement money leaks in three places. In our experience the cause is rarely that the team works too little. Most enablement teams work too much. The leak is spend that never turns into a finished, adopted program.

### Leak 1: platforms paid for and half-used

Software is often bought for every rep and used by far fewer. Zylo's 2026 SaaS Management Index data shows the average organization uses only 54% of its provisioned software licenses. Enablement tools follow the same pattern. In the 2025 Impact of Enablement report from Spekit and the Sales Enablement Collective, 80% of enablement professionals said reps do not use at least 40% of their platform's features. (That report was co-produced by a platform vendor and surveyed 100+ enablement professionals, so read it as directional.)

### Leak 2: programs built and never followed up

A program without practice and reinforcement fades. Memory research has said this for over a century. Murre and Dros's 2015 replication of Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, published in PLOS ONE, reproduced the classic shape: steep loss soon after learning, then a slower decline. The same Spekit and Sales Enablement Collective report found that 24.2% of respondents say more than 80% of the content they create goes unused, and 48.8% say at least 40% of their collateral is out of date.

### Leak 3: skilled people doing production work

The third leak is quieter. Enablement leaders, hired for judgment, spend their weeks formatting slides, loading modules, chasing completion and pulling reports by hand. Those hours are paid at strategist rates and produce work that others could do to the same standard.

## Why didn't AI raise enablement output per dollar?

AI made enablement assets cheap. A battlecard, a script or a roleplay scenario that took a day to draft now takes much less. So output per dollar should be soaring. In many teams it is not.

The reason is that the asset was never the expensive part. The expensive parts are:

- Deciding what the field needs, and in which order.
- Making the asset right: approved claims, your methodology, a quality review.
- Getting it into the tools reps use and launching it properly.
- Making sure reps complete it and managers reinforce it.
- Showing the CRO whether it changed anything.

AI helps with the first draft. It does not run a program, chase completion or sit in a monthly review with a CRO. Teams that put AI-saved hours into more content make the second leak worse. Teams that put them into operations and measurement raise output per dollar.

## How do you link enablement output to revenue?

Link one program at a time to one outcome, using the [four levels of evidence](/glossary/#four-levels-of-evidence): activity, practice, behavior and outcome. Set the baseline before the program, not after.

Three design choices make the link credible:

1. **Choose one outcome per program.** Onboarding links to ramp time. A discovery program links to stage-two conversion. A pricing program links to discount rate.
2. **Use a comparison.** Where you can, start one team 30 days before another similar team and compare them. Where you cannot, compare against the trend from the previous two quarters.
3. **Ask finance for the value of a unit.** Finance should set what one month of faster ramp or one point of win rate is worth. Your number will be trusted more if it is theirs.

The [sales enablement metrics guide](/guides/sales-enablement-metrics/) covers each level of evidence in detail.

## Example: output per dollar and ROI for a 300-rep team

Example: a company with 300 reps spends $900,000 a year on enablement.

| Spend line | Annual cost |
|---|---|
| Three enablement staff, fully loaded | $480,000 |
| LMS, content platform and roleplay tool | $150,000 |
| Enablement share of the kickoff | $200,000 |
| External design and video | $70,000 |
| **Total** | **$900,000** |

**Year 1 outputs:** four programs completed on time, 180 reps certified, 75 reps showing the target behavior on recorded calls.

- Cost per program completed on time: $900,000 ÷ 4 = $225,000.
- Cost per certified rep: $900,000 ÷ 180 = $5,000.
- Cost per rep showing the behavior: $900,000 ÷ 75 = $12,000.

**Year 2, same budget.** The team cuts unused roleplay seats and moves the savings into kickoff follow-up. It hands off formatting and module building, so the enablement leads spend their hours on manager coaching packs. Outputs rise to seven programs completed on time, 255 reps certified and 135 reps showing the behavior.

- Cost per program completed on time: about $129,000.
- Cost per certified rep: about $3,500.
- Cost per rep showing the behavior: about $6,700.

Output per dollar nearly doubled on behaviors seen on calls, with no increase in budget.

**Classic ROI on one program.** The onboarding program cost $200,000 of that budget. The company ran it for 60 new hires and compared them with a cohort hired the previous half-year. The new cohort reached full productivity half a month faster. Finance values one month of a ramped rep's gross profit at $20,000.

- Benefit: 60 hires × 0.5 months × $20,000 = $600,000.
- ROI: ($600,000 − $200,000) ÷ $200,000 × 100 = 200%.

## What are the limits of these numbers?

These numbers are honest only if you state their limits. Comparison cohorts are rarely identical: one may have a better manager or an easier territory. Behavior on calls can only be measured where calls are recorded; elsewhere, use roleplay scores, certifications and manager observations. And small groups produce noisy results, so present results from teams under about 30 reps as indicative, not proven.

## Common mistakes

- **Reporting spend per rep as performance.** It rewards cutting budget, not raising output.
- **Counting what was built instead of what was used.** A program with 40% completion is not an output.
- **Setting the baseline after the program.** You cannot measure change from a starting point you chose afterward.
- **Claiming all revenue growth.** A CFO will discount the whole report. Claim one program's effect, with its method.
- **Putting AI-saved hours into more content.** Put them into launch, reinforcement and measurement instead.

If you want to see how your enablement hours and spend compare with what your plan needs, the free [20-minute Capacity Check](/#capacity-check) gives you a first estimate.

## FAQ

### What is a good ROI for sales enablement?

There is no reliable public benchmark for enablement ROI as a percentage, because methods differ so much. A more useful target is direction: your cost per certified rep and cost per rep showing the target behavior should fall year on year, and at least one program per year should show a measured outcome against a baseline.

### What costs should go into sales enablement ROI?

Include fully loaded enablement salaries, every enablement platform license, content and video production, external agencies or partners, the enablement share of the sales kickoff, and certification or event costs. Exclude rep time in training unless your finance team asks for it, and say clearly which choice you made.

### How long does it take to see ROI from sales enablement?

Activity and practice show within weeks. Behavior on calls usually shows within one to three months if managers reinforce it. Outcomes such as win rate or ramp time need at least one full sales cycle, so for long-cycle enterprise sales expect six to twelve months before outcome data means much.

### Can you prove sales enablement caused a revenue increase?

Rarely with certainty, because pricing, territories, hiring and the market all move at the same time. You can build a credible chain instead: the program, then the behavior seen on calls, then movement in the deals where that behavior appeared, ideally with a staggered start between two similar teams.

### Is cost per rep a good enablement metric?

Total enablement spend per rep is a useful budget check but a poor performance metric, because it rewards spending less rather than delivering more. Cost per certified rep or cost per rep showing a target behavior is better, because it falls when output rises, not only when budget is cut.

## Sources

- [Training Industry: Phillips ROI methodology](https://trainingindustry.com/wiki/measurement-and-analytics/phillips-roi-methodology/)
- [Newswire (Spekit and Sales Enablement Collective): New research reveals the hidden cost of traditional enablement platforms, 2025 Impact of Enablement report](https://www.newswire.com/news/new-research-reveals-the-hidden-cost-of-traditional-enablement-22554701)
- [Zylo: Tracking employee SaaS usage uncovers significant underutilization (2026 SaaS Management Index data)](https://zylo.com/blog/saas-usage-numbers)
- [PLOS ONE: Murre and Dros, Replication and analysis of Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve (2015)](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0120644)
