# How many sales enablement people do you need? The 1:25–50 rule of thumb

> Our rule of thumb is one sales enablement person for every 25 to 50 quota-carrying reps. Divide your rep count by 25 and by 50 to get the range. Move toward 1:25 when you hire many reps, launch often or expect enablement to support coaching. Move toward 1:50 when the sales motion is stable and managers coach on their own.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/sales-enablement-team-size/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- Our rule of thumb: one enablement person supports 25 to 50 quota-carrying reps, depending on onboarding, launch and coaching load.
- Divide your rep count by 25 and by 50; that range is the enablement team your sales plan quietly assumes.
- An hours model is more precise than a ratio: list the work the plan needs, estimate hours per item and divide by about 1,400 productive hours per person.
- A capacity gap does not disappear; it shows up as kickoffs with no follow-up, late launches and new hires who ramp by shadowing.
- No verified public benchmark for the enablement-to-rep ratio exists, so treat any single number, including ours, as a starting point.

Most sales plans size the work for enablement in detail: new hires, launches, a kickoff, certifications. Few size the hours. This guide gives you a quick ratio, a more precise hours model and a worked example, so you can put both numbers on one page before the plan is final.

## What is the rule of thumb for sales enablement team size?

Our rule of thumb is one sales enablement person for every 25 to 50 quota-carrying reps. The low end (1:25) fits teams with heavy onboarding, many launches or enablement-led coaching. The high end (1:50) fits stable teams with experienced managers.

We say "rule of thumb" on purpose. We looked for a public, primary benchmark on the [enablement-to-rep ratio](/glossary/#enablement-to-rep-ratio) and did not find one we could verify. Several vendor blogs quote ratios in the same range, but none publishes a method or sample. Treat any single ratio, including ours, as a starting point to test against your own hours.

What the public data does show is pressure on headcount. The Sales Enablement Collective's 2025 landscape report found that 23.6% of respondents' teams shrank over the previous 12 months. Sales plans rarely shrank by the same amount.

## How do you do the arithmetic?

Count your quota-carrying reps. Divide by 25, then by 50. That is the range of enablement people your sales plan assumes. Then count the people you actually have.

| Quota-carrying reps | At 1:50 | At 1:25 |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 2 | 4 |
| 200 | 4 | 8 |
| 300 | 6 | 12 |
| 500 | 10 | 20 |
| 1,000 | 20 | 40 |

If the plan assumes four to eight people and you have two, the gap does not disappear. It is not a judgment of the enablement team. It is a planning error: the work was sized and the hours were not.

You can run your own numbers in the [enablement capacity calculator](/tools/enablement-capacity-calculator/).

## What moves you toward 1:25 and what moves you toward 1:50?

Five drivers decide where you sit in the range. Score each from 0 to 2, then add them up. This is our working heuristic, not a published standard.

| Driver | 0 points | 1 point | 2 points |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hiring volume (new hires per year as a share of reps) | Under 15% | 15–30% | Over 30% |
| Launches and major message changes per year | 0–1 | 2–3 | 4 or more |
| Coaching load | Managers coach on their own | Enablement provides coaching packs | Enablement runs scored roleplays and weekly coaching cards |
| Complexity (segments, product lines, languages) | One motion, one language | Two or three | Four or more |
| Production help (designers, video, LMS admin) | Full in-house or partner support | Partial | None |

**How to read the score:**

- **0–3 points:** plan near 1:50.
- **4–6 points:** plan near 1:35 to 1:40.
- **7–10 points:** plan near 1:25.

Hiring volume carries the most weight in practice, because onboarding work scales with every new hire. The Bridge Group's 2026 AE report, covering 158 B2B companies, found average AE ramp time of 6.2 months, the highest in the study's history. Longer ramps mean each cohort of new hires needs enablement support for longer.

Coaching load is the driver most teams underestimate. Gartner's 2024 survey of 1,026 B2B sellers found that 72% feel overwhelmed by the number of skills their job requires. Teaching a skill once is not enough. Someone has to build the practice, the scorecard and the manager materials that keep it alive.

## How do you size enablement by hours instead of headcount?

An hours model is more precise than a ratio. List the work the sales plan needs, estimate hours for each item, add them up and divide by the productive hours of one enablement person.

These are our planning assumptions. Replace them with your own history where you have it.

| Work item | Planning assumption |
|---|---|
| Productive hours per enablement person per year | 1,400 (after meetings, leave and admin) |
| Onboarding, per new hire | 30 hours (cohort sessions, certification review, updates) |
| Product or message launch | 300 hours each |
| Sales kickoff plus 90-day follow-up | 1,000 hours |
| Skill program or certification | 300 hours each |
| Coaching support | 6 hours per sales manager per month |
| Content upkeep, tool admin and reporting | 6 hours per rep per year |

The kickoff line includes the follow-up on purpose. Many teams budget the event and forget the 90 days after it. See [after the sales kickoff](/guides/sales-kickoff-follow-up/) for what those 90 days need.

## Example: sizing enablement for a 300-rep team

Example: a software company has 300 quota-carrying reps and 30 sales managers. Next year's plan includes 90 new hires, four product launches, one kickoff and three skill programs. The enablement team has three people.

| Work item | Calculation | Hours |
|---|---|---|
| Onboarding | 90 hires × 30 | 2,700 |
| Launches | 4 × 300 | 1,200 |
| Kickoff and 90-day follow-up | 1 × 1,000 | 1,000 |
| Skill programs | 3 × 300 | 900 |
| Coaching support | 30 managers × 6 × 12 months | 2,160 |
| Content, tools and reporting | 300 reps × 6 | 1,800 |
| **Total needed** | | **9,760** |

The plan needs 9,760 hours. Divided by 1,400 hours per person, that is about seven people, or one per 43 reps. That sits inside the 1:25–50 range.

The team has three people, or 4,200 hours. The gap is 5,560 hours, roughly four people.

Now run the same company in a high-growth year: 150 new hires, six launches and four skill programs. The total rises to 12,460 hours, about nine people, or one per 34 reps. The ratio moved toward 1:25 because hiring and launches grew, not because the rep count did.

If your hours model lands outside 1:25–50, trust the hours model. The ratio is a quick check. The hours are the plan.

## Who should be on a sales enablement team?

A sales enablement team needs a mix of strategy, production and operations skills, not five copies of the same role. The ratio tells you how many people; the mix decides what they can deliver.

| Role | Main work | When to add it |
|---|---|---|
| Head of enablement | Priorities with the CRO, program design, results | First hire |
| Program manager | Onboarding, launches, skill programs end to end | From about 75 reps |
| Content and instructional designer | Assets, modules, roleplay scenarios | When launches or onboarding outgrow the leader's time |
| Enablement operations | Platform admin, launches, nudges, reporting | When you run two or more enablement tools |

Many teams of three are three program managers. They spend a large share of their week on production and operations, because nobody else does it. A designer or an operations role, in-house or through a partner, often adds more delivered programs than a fourth program manager would.

## What are your options when the team is too small?

You have five options, and most teams combine two or three.

| Option | What it does | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Cut scope | Agree three priority behaviors with the CRO and drop the rest | Some requests go unmet; you must say no in writing |
| Hire | Adds permanent capacity | Slow to recruit and ramp; fixed cost |
| Borrow manager time | Managers run roleplays and coaching | Competes with selling time; quality varies |
| Buy tools | Automates some delivery | Tools need someone to fill and run them |
| Hand off production and operations | Frees enablement hours for strategy | Needs a clear brief, approval process and partner standards |

Buying a tool is the option most often chosen and least often sufficient. A platform adds a second job: running it. The [outsourced sales enablement guide](/guides/outsourced-sales-enablement/) covers which work you can hand off safely.

## What does the ratio not tell you?

The ratio does not tell you about skill mix, quality or where hours actually go. Three limits are worth stating plainly.

- **Two teams with the same ratio can perform very differently.** A team of five strategists with no production help may deliver less than a team of three with a designer and an LMS administrator.
- **It ignores other audiences.** If enablement also supports SDRs, sales engineers or customer success, count them, weighted by their program load.
- **AI changes the production hours, not the operations hours.** Drafting is faster. Launching, chasing completion, supporting managers and reporting take about as long as before.

## What to do this quarter

1. Count your quota-carrying reps and divide by 25 and by 50.
2. Score the five drivers to see where in the range you belong.
3. List next year's planned hires, launches, kickoff and programs, and estimate hours with the table above.
4. Count your team's productive hours (people × 1,400).
5. Put the hours needed and the hours available on one slide for your CRO, with the three options you recommend to close the gap.
6. Use the result as the first input to your [12-month enablement roadmap](/guides/sales-enablement-roadmap/).

If you want a second opinion on your numbers, a free [20-minute Capacity Check](/#capacity-check) with your CRO and head of enablement produces a capacity estimate you can keep.

## FAQ

### What is a good sales enablement to rep ratio?

Our rule of thumb is 1:25 to 1:50. Fast-growing teams with heavy onboarding, frequent launches or enablement-led coaching need the richer end. Stable teams with experienced managers can run near 1:50. We have not found a primary, audited benchmark, so validate the ratio with an hours model.

### Do sales engineers and customer success managers count as reps?

Count every role that enablement is expected to train and support. If enablement also onboards sales engineers, SDRs or customer success managers, include them, but weight them by how much program work they need. A team that supports 200 sellers and 100 customer success managers has a larger load than one with 200 sellers alone.

### How many sales reps can one enablement manager support?

One experienced enablement manager can usually support 25 to 50 reps when they own the full cycle of building, launching, reinforcing and reporting programs. With dedicated production help, from a designer, an instructional designer or a partner, the same person can cover more reps because their hours go to strategy and stakeholder work.

### Should the first enablement hire be a strategist or a producer?

Hire for judgment first: someone who can agree priorities with the CRO and design programs. Production can be added later through junior hires, contractors or a partner. A producer without a strategy owner tends to build whatever is requested, which fills the calendar without changing behavior.

### Does AI reduce how many enablement people you need?

AI cuts the time to draft assets, so production hours drop. It does little for operations: launching programs, chasing completion, supporting managers and reporting. In our experience the ratio moves a little toward 1:50, not to 1:100, because the work AI removes was rarely the bottleneck.

### What happens if the enablement team is too small?

The work the plan needs still exists, so it shows up elsewhere. Common signs are a kickoff with no follow-up, launches reps learn from a slide deck, new hires who ramp by shadowing whoever has time, and tools that sit half-used.

## Sources

- [Sales Enablement Collective: Sales enablement salary and landscape report 2025](https://www.salesenablementcollective.com/sales-enablement-salary-and-landscape-report/)
- [The Bridge Group: 2026 AE models, motions and metrics](https://www.bridgegroupinc.com/research/2026-ae-models-motions-metrics)
- [Gartner: Gartner sales survey reveals sellers who partner with AI are 3.7 times more likely to meet quota (September 2024)](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2024-09-16-gartner-sales-survey-reveals-sellers-who-partner-with-ai-re-three-point-seven-times-more-likely-to-meet-quota)

# Sales enablement vs sales training: what's the difference?

> Sales training builds skills and knowledge through programs such as courses, workshops, roleplays and certifications. Sales enablement is the wider, ongoing discipline that gives sellers and their managers what they need to sell well: training plus content, tools, coaching, onboarding and measurement. Training is one service inside enablement, usually the largest, but rarely enough on its own.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/sales-enablement-vs-sales-training/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- Sales training builds skills; sales enablement makes sure those skills, plus the right content and tools, show up in real buyer conversations.
- Training is one service inside sales enablement, and CSO Insights found it was the most common enablement service for four years running.
- Training is an event or a program with an end date; enablement is an ongoing system with a roadmap.
- If reps can pass the roleplay but do not do it on calls, you have an enablement problem, not a training problem.
- Revenue enablement extends the same discipline to every customer-facing role, not only sellers.

Sales enablement and sales training are often used as if they mean the same thing. They do not, and the confusion has a cost: companies buy a training program to fix a problem that training cannot fix, then wonder why nothing changed on calls. This guide gives a plain definition of each, a side-by-side comparison, a way to decide which one you need, and how the two work together.

## What is the difference between sales enablement and sales training?

Sales training builds skills and knowledge. Sales enablement is the wider discipline that makes sure those skills, plus the right content, tools and coaching, show up in real buyer conversations. Training is one service inside enablement.

CSO Insights, in its 2019 Sales Enablement Report, defined sales enablement as a strategic, collaborative discipline that provides consistent, scalable services so that customer-facing professionals and their managers can add value in every customer interaction. The same report described sales training as covering selling skills, sales methodologies, sales processes, sales technology and product training, delivered through e-learning, classroom, online and hybrid formats.

Put simply: training answers "can the rep do it?" Enablement answers "does the rep do it, with the right support, on real deals, and can we prove it?" For a longer definition, see [what is sales enablement](/guides/what-is-sales-enablement/).

## Sales enablement vs sales training: side by side

| Dimension | Sales training | Sales enablement |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Build a skill or knowledge | Improve sales results through skills, content, tools and coaching |
| Scope | Courses, workshops, roleplays, certifications | Training plus onboarding, content, talk tracks, battlecards, tools, manager coaching support, measurement |
| Shape over time | Event or program with an end date | Ongoing system with a 12-month roadmap |
| Typical owner | Sales training lead, L&D or an outside provider | Head of enablement, reporting to sales or revenue leadership |
| Audience | Reps, sometimes managers | Reps, managers and other customer-facing roles |
| Main measures | Attendance, completion, quiz and certification scores | Ramp time, behavior on calls, content adoption, stage conversion, win rate |
| Main tools | LMS, roleplay tool, classroom | LMS, content platform, roleplay tool, conversation intelligence, CRM |
| Common failure | Skill learned, then forgotten | Too many services, none finished or measured |

## Is sales training part of sales enablement?

Yes. Sales training is the most common service enablement teams provide. The CSO Insights 2019 report found that training services ranked first among enablement services for four years in a row, followed by sales tools. Onboarding ranked sixth and coaching by the enablement team seventh.

The same report made the key point: training can start a change, but it cannot reach enablement's goals alone. It needs ongoing coaching to become effective. Training-transfer research agrees. In Alan Saks and Monica Belcourt's 2006 study of 150 organizations, training professionals estimated that about 62% of trainees applied training immediately, but only 34% a year later. Activities before and after training were more strongly related to transfer than activities during it. Enablement is the "before and after".

## When do you need sales training, and when do you need sales enablement?

You need training when the gap is a skill or knowledge gap and the rest of the system works. You need enablement when the skill exists but does not show up on calls, or when the gap is content, tools, onboarding or measurement. Use this table to diagnose.

| Situation | What you need | Why |
|---|---|---|
| New product launch; reps do not know it yet | Training, inside an enablement launch plan | Knowledge gap, but reps also need talk tracks and battlecards |
| Reps pass the roleplay but do not do it on calls | Enablement: manager reinforcement and call checks | The skill exists; the transfer is missing |
| Reps cannot find the right content in deals | Enablement: content operations | Not a skill gap |
| New hires take more than seven months to ramp | Enablement: an onboarding system, with training inside it | Ramp depends on territory, tools, plan and manager, not only courses |
| One cohort is weak at one skill | Training: a targeted [skill sprint](/guides/continuous-sales-training/) | Narrow, well-defined skill gap |
| The CRO asks what changed after last year's training | Enablement: measurement | Training reports activity; the CRO needs behavior and outcomes |
| A new sales methodology is being adopted | Both | Training teaches it; enablement embeds it in content, CRM and coaching |

## How do sales enablement and sales training work together?

They work as one loop. Enablement diagnoses the gap and sets the priority. Training builds the skill. Content and tools support it in the flow of work. Managers reinforce it. Measurement checks whether it shows up on calls and in deals, and picks the next gap.

1. **Diagnose:** enablement finds the behavior gap from calls, deals and roleplay scores, by cohort.
2. **Build the skill:** training delivers practice, scored against a shared scorecard.
3. **Support the moment:** talk tracks, battlecards and examples are available where reps work.
4. **Reinforce:** managers coach the skill on live deals and ask about practice.
5. **Measure:** results are reported at four levels: activity, practice, behavior and outcome. See [sales enablement metrics](/guides/sales-enablement-metrics/).

Training without steps 1, 3, 4 and 5 is an event. Enablement without step 2 is a content library.

## Does formal sales enablement improve results?

Survey data suggests it does, when it is formal. In the CSO Insights 2019 report, based on more than 900 participants, organizations with sales enablement reported a 49.0% win rate on forecast deals, against 42.5% for those without. Organizations with a formal enablement approach and a written charter reported 55.1%, against 39.2% for those with a random, project-by-project approach. Only 15.8% of organizations were in the formal-and-charter group. These are correlations, but the pattern held across years of the study.

The discipline is also widening. In 2023, Gartner said it expected 60% of enablement functions to be tasked with enabling all client-facing, revenue-generating roles by 2026, which it calls revenue enablement. Gartner's 2024 Market Guide described revenue enablement platforms as broadened from sales enablement to deliver content, learning and coaching to revenue-generating roles. See the [glossary entry for revenue enablement](/glossary/#revenue-enablement).

## Who should own sales training when you have an enablement team?

Enablement should own the sales training plan and how it is measured, even when others deliver parts of it. Delivery can come from several places, and that is fine:

- **Enablement** designs and runs skill programs, certifications and roleplays tied to the sales process.
- **Product marketing** supplies product knowledge and competitive content, reviewed by enablement for the sales context.
- **L&D** often owns company-wide skills, leadership and compliance programs, and may run sales manager development.
- **Sales leaders and top reps** teach real examples from current deals.
- **Outside providers** bring a methodology or extra production capacity.

The rule is one plan, one scorecard and one owner of the results. When three teams train reps on three different frameworks in the same quarter, reps learn that none of them matters. A written enablement charter, with services, audiences and measures, is the simplest way to settle ownership.

## Example: the same product launch, run two ways

Example: a 200-rep company launches a new product.

| | Training only | Enablement with training inside |
|---|---|---|
| What happens | Two-hour virtual session, recorded | Same session, plus a certification in week one, one roleplay per use case, a talk track and battlecard in the CRM, a manager coaching guide and a call check at day 60 |
| Enablement hours | About 40 | About 140 |
| What you can report at day 60 | 92% attended | 92% attended, 81% certified, new product mentioned on 30% of relevant calls, 45 opportunities created |
| What the CRO learns | The session happened | Whether reps are selling it, and which teams are not |

The extra 100 hours buy the evidence. Without them, the launch report says only that people attended.

## Common mistakes

- **Buying training to fix a transfer problem.** If reps can do it in the roleplay, more training will not change calls.
- **Calling the training team "enablement" without changing its scope.** A new name with the same services and measures changes nothing.
- **Measuring enablement by training completion.** Completion is the first of four levels, not the result.
- **Splitting ownership without a single plan.** When L&D, product marketing and sales each train reps separately, reps get mixed messages. One owner should hold the plan.

## What are the limits of this distinction?

The line between training and enablement blurs in small teams, where one person does both. That is fine, as long as someone owns the full loop from diagnosis to measurement. The survey data cited here shows association, not cause. And enablement cannot fix a weak product, a bad territory plan or a broken compensation plan. To plan both together, start with a [12-month sales enablement roadmap](/guides/sales-enablement-roadmap/).

If you want to see how much enablement work your plan needs beyond training, book a free [20-minute Capacity Check](/#capacity-check).

## FAQ

### Is sales training part of sales enablement?

Yes. Sales training is one of the services sales enablement provides, alongside content, tools, onboarding, coaching support and measurement. In most enablement teams it is the largest single service.

### What is the difference between sales enablement and L&D?

Learning and development usually serves the whole company with general skills, leadership and compliance programs. Sales enablement serves customer-facing roles with programs tied to the sales process, buyer and pipeline, and it measures results in sales terms such as ramp time and win rate.

### Do I need sales enablement or sales training?

If you have a specific, well-defined skill gap and managers ready to reinforce it, a training program may be enough. If reps cannot find content, ramp slowly, or pass training but do not change on calls, you need enablement.

### What is revenue enablement?

Revenue enablement applies the sales enablement discipline to every revenue-generating role, such as customer success, presales, partners and marketing, not only sellers. Gartner expected 60% of enablement functions to be tasked with enabling all client-facing, revenue-generating roles by 2026.

### Who should own sales training if there is an enablement team?

Enablement should own the sales training plan and its measurement. Delivery can come from enablement, L&D, product marketing, sales leaders or outside providers, but one owner should decide what gets trained, in what order, and how it is reinforced.

### Can sales training work without sales enablement?

It can teach a skill, but it often fades. Without content that supports the skill, manager reinforcement and a check of real calls, most of what was trained is not used months later.

## Sources

- [CSO Insights (Miller Heiman Group): 2019 Sales Enablement Report](https://community.highspot.com/assets/2019/10/CSO-Insights-5th-Annual-Sales-Enablement-Study.pdf)
- [Gartner: How Revenue Enablement Helps Sales Organizations Exceed Performance Targets (2023)](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2023-05-17-how-revenue-enablement-helps-sales-organizations-exceed-performance-targets)
- [Gartner: Market Guide for Revenue Enablement Platforms (2024)](https://www.gartner.com/en/documents/5654123)
- [Human Resource Management: Saks and Belcourt, An Investigation of Training Activities and Transfer of Training in Organizations (2006)](https://doi.org/10.1002/hrm.20135)

# After the sales kickoff: a 90-day reinforcement plan

> A sales kickoff follow-up plan turns the event into behavior on calls. Certify every rep on the core message within 14 days, run one scored roleplay per new play with a scorecard managers also use, nudge non-starters weekly with a list for each manager, and report activity, practice and call behavior to the CRO at days 30, 60 and 90.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/sales-kickoff-follow-up/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- The kickoff gets the budget, but the 90 days after it decide whether the money pays off.
- Certify every rep on the core message within 14 days, while the event is still fresh.
- Build one scored roleplay per new play and give managers the same scorecard reps are scored on.
- Report to the CRO at days 30, 60 and 90 with activity, practice, behavior on calls and early outcomes.
- Our rule of thumb: plan as many enablement hours for the 90 days after the kickoff as for building the event.

Every year, sales organizations spend heavily on a kickoff: new messaging, new plays, a big room and a lot of energy. Then the next month starts. The event gets the budget, and the 90 days after it get almost nothing: no practice, no manager follow-up and no check of whether the new message is used on calls. This guide gives you a week-by-week plan for those 90 days, the reports your CRO should see, and a worked example with hours and numbers.

## Why does sales kickoff content fade so fast?

Kickoff content fades because people forget quickly after a single exposure, and nothing in the weeks after the event asks reps to use what they heard. Memory research and training-transfer research point the same way.

The forgetting curve is real and has been replicated. In 2015, Jaap Murre and Joeri Dros repeated Hermann Ebbinghaus's 1880s experiment and published it in PLOS ONE. Their results closely matched the original: forgetting is fastest soon after learning, and the rate slows over time. The limit: it was one subject learning nonsense syllables, not a seller learning a talk track. But the shape is the useful part. A message heard once in January is mostly gone by March unless it is used again.

Spacing helps. A 2006 meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin by Nicholas Cepeda and colleagues reviewed 839 assessments from 317 experiments. It found that spreading study sessions out improves retention, and that the best gap between sessions grows as the time you need to remember grows. For a kickoff, that means practice spread over weeks, not one more session on day two.

Work-environment support matters most. Alan Saks and Monica Belcourt surveyed training professionals in 150 organizations (Human Resource Management, 2006). Their respondents estimated that about 62% of trainees applied training immediately, 44% after six months and 34% after a year. The authors also found that activities before and after training were more strongly related to transfer than activities during it. These are estimates by training staff, not observed behavior, but the direction is clear: the follow-up does more than the event.

## Who should own the 90 days after the kickoff?

The head of enablement should own the plan and the reports, front-line managers should own practice and coaching for their reps, and the CRO should sponsor it. Name all three before the kickoff. If the owners are named afterward, the plan usually starts in week four, when most of the forgetting has already happened.

Budget the hours at the same time as the event. Our rule of thumb: plan as many enablement hours for the 90 days after the kickoff as for building the kickoff itself. If your team cannot cover both, the [enablement capacity calculator](/tools/enablement-capacity-calculator/) shows the gap in hours before it shows up as a kickoff with no follow-up.

## The 90-day kickoff reinforcement plan, week by week

The plan has four parts: a short certification in the first two weeks, one roleplay per new play, weekly nudges with a list for each manager, and a CRO report at days 30, 60 and 90. The table shows when each part runs.

| Window | What happens | Owner | Evidence produced |
|---|---|---|---|
| Weeks -4 to 0 | Agree the three behaviors the kickoff must change. Build the certification and roleplays. Pull a baseline from recorded calls or manager observation. | Enablement, CRO | Baseline for behavior and stage conversion |
| Kickoff week | CRO announces the certification on stage. Certification opens on the last day of the event. | CRO, enablement | Launch message sent |
| Days 1–14 | Every rep completes the certification on the core message. Nudges on days 3, 7 and 10. Manager lists every Monday. | Enablement, managers | Certification rate and scores |
| Weeks 3–6 | One scored roleplay per new play, one play a week. Managers use the same scorecard in one-to-ones. | Managers, enablement | Practice attempts and scores per play |
| Day 30 | First CRO report: activity and practice. | Head of enablement | One-page report |
| Weeks 5–8 | Managers coach one live deal per rep using the new plays. Enablement checks a sample of recorded calls. | Managers, enablement | Coaching coverage, call evidence |
| Day 60 | Second CRO report: adds behavior on calls. | Head of enablement | One-page report |
| Weeks 9–12 | Retest the bottom quartile. Run a second, spaced round of the hardest roleplay. | Enablement, managers | Score change since day 14 |
| Day 90 | Third CRO report: adds early outcome indicators. Plays move into the normal coaching rhythm. | Head of enablement | One-page report, next-quarter plan |

### Certification in the first 14 days

Test the situation, not the knowledge. A good kickoff certification asks the rep to deliver the core message to a realistic buyer: a recorded two-minute opening, or a short roleplay where the buyer pushes back once. Score it from 0 to 100 on three behaviors, with a pass line at 70. A quiz about the new messaging framework tells you who can recognize the right answer. It does not tell you who will say it to a CFO. See the [glossary entry on certification](/glossary/#certification) for the difference.

### One roleplay per new play

If the kickoff introduced three plays, build three roleplays, and release one a week. Each roleplay uses the same three-behavior scorecard that managers use when they listen to calls. One shared scorecard is what turns practice into coaching: the rep, the roleplay tool and the manager are all grading the same thing.

### Nudges and manager lists

Send reps who have not started a short nudge on days 3, 7 and 10, from their sales leader rather than from "Enablement". Send each manager a list every Monday: who has not started, who failed, who scored highest. If completion is below 80% at day 14, escalate to the second-line manager. Most completion problems are manager problems, and a manager who sees a named list acts faster than one who sees a percentage.

## What should the day 30, 60 and 90 reports to the CRO show?

Each report adds one level of evidence. Day 30 shows activity and practice. Day 60 adds behavior on real calls. Day 90 adds early outcomes. This follows the [four levels of evidence](/guides/sales-enablement-metrics/) and fits on one page.

| Report | Activity | Practice | Behavior | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Day 30 | Certification completion by team | Certification pass rate, roleplay attempts per play | Not yet | Not yet |
| Day 60 | Roleplay completion by team | Average score per play, change since day 14 | Share of sampled calls where the new message is heard, against baseline | Not yet |
| Day 90 | Final completion | Retest results for the bottom quartile | Call evidence by team, coaching coverage | Stage conversion for opportunities where the play was used, against baseline |

Report by team, not by rep. A CRO needs to see where adoption is weak, and managers need a shared goal rather than a ranking. The [one-page CRO report](/guides/enablement-report-for-cro/) guide has a template.

## Example: a 300-rep kickoff, followed up for 90 days

Example: a company with 300 reps and 30 managers runs a kickoff that introduces three new plays. The kickoff costs $1.2 million, or $4,000 per rep, including travel.

- **Before the event:** enablement samples 120 recorded discovery calls. The new problem-first opening is heard on 12% of them. This is the baseline.
- **Day 14:** 255 reps have passed certification (85%). Two teams are below 60%, and their second-line manager gets the list.
- **Day 30:** 210 reps (70%) have completed at least two of the three roleplays. Average score on the hardest play is 61.
- **Day 60:** a new sample of 120 calls shows the opening on 38% of calls, against the 12% baseline. Managers documented coaching on a live deal for 60% of reps.
- **Day 90:** the retested bottom quartile moved from an average of 52 to 68. Discovery-to-proposal conversion is reported against last year's same quarter, with the caveat that other things changed too.

The follow-up took about 180 enablement hours: 40 to build the certification, 60 for three roleplays, 36 for nudges and manager lists (3 hours a week for 12 weeks), 24 for three reports and 20 for a manager coaching pack. That is roughly a third of one enablement person's quarter. At a fully loaded rate of $150 an hour, it costs about $27,000, or just over 2% of the event.

Now compare the cost per rep who uses the message. If 30% of reps use the new opening without follow-up, the kickoff cost $13,333 per rep who changed. If the follow-up lifts that to 60%, the cost falls to about $6,667. The hours are small next to the event.

## Common mistakes

- **Starting the follow-up after the event.** If the certification and roleplays are built in February, the plan starts when most of the forgetting has already happened. Build them before the kickoff.
- **Testing knowledge instead of delivery.** A quiz pass rate looks good on a slide and predicts very little about calls.
- **Giving managers a dashboard instead of a list.** Managers act on names and one clear ask, not on a new login.
- **Reporting only completion.** A 94% completion rate says the program was delivered. It does not say the message reached a single customer.
- **Skipping the baseline.** Without a pre-kickoff measure of call behavior, the day 60 number has nothing to beat.

## What are the limits of this plan?

The plan shows a believable chain from kickoff to calls, not proof that the kickoff caused a change in win rate. Seasonality, new hires and pricing changes all move outcomes in the same quarter. Behavior evidence also depends on recorded calls. Where calls are not recorded, use roleplay scores, manager observations and CRM stage data, and say so in the report. And the plan needs managers who show up. If managers will not coach for 30 minutes a week, read [why sales training fades without managers](/guides/sales-manager-reinforcement/) before you plan the next event, and track [coaching coverage](/guides/sales-coaching-coverage/) from day one.

If you are not sure your team has the hours to run the 90 days after your next kickoff, a free [20-minute Capacity Check](/#capacity-check) will show you the gap.

## FAQ

### How long should sales kickoff reinforcement last?

Plan for 90 days. That is long enough for reps to use the new message on real calls and for managers to coach it, and short enough to keep the focus. After day 90, fold the plays into your normal skill sprints and coaching rhythm.

### What is a sales kickoff certification?

It is a short, scored test of whether a rep can deliver the core message in a realistic situation, such as a recorded two-minute pitch or a roleplay with a scripted buyer. It is not a quiz. Run it in the first 14 days and set a clear pass line, such as 70 out of 100.

### How do you measure whether a sales kickoff worked?

Measure four levels: activity (who completed), practice (who passed certification and roleplays), behavior (is the new message heard on recorded calls) and outcome (did stage conversion or win rate move). Set the baseline before the kickoff, or you will have nothing to compare against.

### Who should own the follow-up after a sales kickoff?

The head of enablement owns the plan and the reporting. Front-line managers own their reps' practice and coaching. The CRO sponsors it and reads the day 30, 60 and 90 reports. Name these owners before the kickoff, not after.

### What if we do not record sales calls?

Use roleplay scores, certification results, manager observations from ride-alongs or call shadowing, and CRM stage data. The behavior evidence is weaker, but you can still show a believable chain from practice to pipeline.

### How much time does a 90-day kickoff follow-up take?

For a team of about 300 reps, our estimate is 150 to 200 enablement hours across the quarter, plus about 30 minutes a week from each manager. Most of the hours go into building certification and roleplays, which can be done before the event.

## Sources

- [PLOS ONE: Murre and Dros, Replication and Analysis of Ebbinghaus' Forgetting Curve (2015)](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0120644)
- [Psychological Bulletin: Cepeda et al., Distributed Practice in Verbal Recall Tasks (2006)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16719566/)
- [Human Resource Management: Saks and Belcourt, An Investigation of Training Activities and Transfer of Training in Organizations (2006)](https://doi.org/10.1002/hrm.20135)
- [CSO Insights (Miller Heiman Group): 2019 Sales Enablement Report](https://community.highspot.com/assets/2019/10/CSO-Insights-5th-Annual-Sales-Enablement-Study.pdf)

# Why sales training fades without managers, and the six manager jobs that fix it

> Sales training fades because reps judge what matters by what their manager asks about. Training-transfer research finds that support at work predicts whether skills get used. Six manager jobs fix it: endorse the program out loud, set one focus skill, coach one live deal a week, ask for the practice score, read numbers by cohort, and escalate stuck reps.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/sales-manager-reinforcement/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- Reps decide whether training matters by watching what their manager asks about in the weekly one-to-one.
- Research on training transfer finds that support in the work environment after training predicts whether skills get used.
- The six manager jobs are endorse, focus, coach, ask, read and escalate.
- The six jobs take a manager with ten reps about 60 to 90 minutes a week if enablement prepares the inputs.
- Design the manager's view of a program first; the rep's view follows.

A well-built sales training program can fade within weeks. The content is fine, the launch goes well, and usage drops after week two. The most common cause is not the program. It is that the rep's manager never asks about it. This guide explains why managers decide whether training sticks, what the research says, and the six manager jobs that make reinforcement happen in about an hour a week.

## Why does sales training fade without manager reinforcement?

Sales training fades because reps judge what matters by what their manager asks about. If the manager never mentions a program in the weekly one-to-one, the rep concludes it does not matter, and the rep is right. Research on training transfer supports this.

A 2010 meta-analysis by Brian Blume, Kevin Ford, Timothy Baldwin and Jason Huang in the Journal of Management pooled 89 studies on what predicts whether training gets used at work. A supportive work environment was among the factors positively related to transfer. The authors also found that factors like motivation and work environment had stronger links to transfer for "open" skills, such as leadership, than for "closed" skills, such as learning software. Selling is an open skill: there is no single right answer, so the environment around the rep matters more.

Alan Saks and Monica Belcourt's 2006 study of 150 organizations in Human Resource Management found that activities in the work environment before and after training were more strongly related to transfer than activities during it. Their respondents, who were training professionals, estimated that only about a third of trainees still applied training a year later.

Sales-specific research points the same way. A 2025 working paper by Johannes Habel, Michael Ahearne and colleagues, posted on SSRN, studied almost 2,000 salespeople at a large US industrial firm. AI roleplay training lifted performance by about 2% on average. Gains were larger for reps with weaker prior performance, and larger when their supervisors were high performers or had a narrow span of control. In plain terms: the same tool did more under managers who had the skill and the time to back it.

The gap is often a relationship gap. The CSO Insights 2019 Sales Enablement Report found that 73.7% of respondents said they include front-line managers in their enablement efforts. The same report noted that enablement leaders often have almost no relationship with those managers.

## Is the tool or the manager the problem when usage drops?

In our experience, the manager layer breaks first. Think of any practice program as four layers. The tool is the layer procurement can see, so it gets the attention. Under it is frequency: one practice session at launch changes nothing. Under that is scoring: without a number to beat, practice feels like homework. At the root is reinforcement: a manager who asks, "What did you score on the pricing scenario?" The software is usually the cheapest layer of the four. When usage drops, check the root before you replace the tool.

## The six manager jobs that make training stick

The six jobs are endorse, focus, coach, ask, read and escalate. Each one is small. Together they tell every rep, every week, that the program matters.

1. **Endorse: approve it out loud.** The manager tells the team what to use and when. "Do the pricing roleplay before your Thursday call." An endorsement from the manager carries more weight than any launch email from enablement.
2. **Focus: set one skill for the next six weeks.** One skill per team per wave. A manager who coaches five things at once teaches none of them. See [continuous sales training](/guides/continuous-sales-training/) for the six-week sprint.
3. **Coach: one live deal a week using the skill.** Pick one rep's real opportunity and coach the focus skill on it. Coaching on the rep's own deal feels like help; coaching on a scripted scenario feels like school.
4. **Ask: for the practice score.** One question in the one-to-one: "What did you score this week?" Just asking changes behavior.
5. **Read: the numbers by cohort, against a benchmark.** Look at team scores against a line, such as 70 out of 100, once a week. An organization-wide average hides the team that is struggling.
6. **Escalate: reps stuck after two rounds.** If a rep has practiced twice and is still below the line, the manager flags it to enablement for a targeted session, instead of waiting for the quarterly review.

| Job | What the manager does | Time per week (10 reps) | Evidence it happened |
|---|---|---|---|
| Endorse | Names the program and the deadline in the team meeting | 5 minutes | Practice starts within 3 days |
| Focus | Confirms the one skill for this wave | 5 minutes (once per wave) | Focus skill set in the coaching log |
| Coach | One live-deal coaching session | 30–45 minutes | Logged coaching conversation with evidence |
| Ask | One question per one-to-one | 10 minutes in total | Practice frequency per rep |
| Read | Reviews the team's scores against the line | 10 minutes | Manager opens the weekly list |
| Escalate | Flags reps below the line after two attempts | 5 minutes | Escalation list to enablement |

Total: about 60 to 90 minutes a week, inside meetings the manager already runs. That estimate assumes enablement prepares the inputs. Without the lists and scores, the same jobs can take three to four hours, and they do not happen.

## Design the manager's view first

The most-used rep tools have one thing in common: the manager uses them too. When you design a program, start with what the manager sees and does each week, then design the rep's experience. If the manager's view is an afterthought, the rep's view gets opened twice and forgotten.

Managers are the most overloaded people in a sales organization. Whatever enablement gives them must take minutes, not hours, and live where they already work: in Slack or Teams, in the CRM, or in the one-to-one agenda. A weekly package for each manager should contain:

- A named list: who has not started, who is below the line, who improved most.
- One question to ask in every one-to-one this week.
- A draft coaching note per rep: one strength, one gap, one drill.
- The team's score against the benchmark, by cohort.

## What must exist before an AI coach helps?

An AI coach or roleplay tool works only on top of four layers, built from the bottom up. First, a manager who uses it every week, not just someone who approved the purchase. Second, real deals, so practice is built from the rep's own opportunities. Third, one skill at a time. Fourth, a score to beat, such as 0 to 100 with a benchmark line. Only then does the AI coach add value, and it should live inside tools reps already open. Most rollouts start at the top and wonder why usage fades in week three. You do not need all four layers perfect, but you need the first. For more, see [AI roleplay for sales training](/guides/ai-roleplay-sales-training/).

## Example: the chain from 100 trained reps to 5 changed reps

Example: these rates are illustrative, to show the shape of the chain. Use your own numbers.

| Step | Without manager jobs | With the six manager jobs |
|---|---|---|
| Reps trained | 100 | 100 |
| Completed the program | 94 | 95 |
| Tried the skill in a roleplay at least once | 60 | 85 |
| Practiced weekly for the wave | 15 | 45 |
| Had a manager ask about it in one-to-ones | 8 | 70 |
| Showed the behavior on real calls afterward | 5 | 25 |

The completion report shows 94% in both columns. The difference is invisible until you follow the chain to behavior on calls. In most teams, the biggest drop is from practicing once to practicing weekly, and the manager's question is what closes it. This is why [measuring sales training effectiveness](/guides/measuring-sales-training-effectiveness/) has to go past completion.

## How do you get busy managers to do the six jobs?

Make the manager's own leader ask the same questions. If a second-line manager asks each first-line manager, "Who on your team is below the line, and what are you doing about it?", the six jobs get done. Add three more rules: put the jobs into the existing one-to-one agenda instead of a new meeting; report results by team, not by manager, so it is a shared goal; and track [coaching coverage](/guides/sales-coaching-coverage/) as the single measure of whether the coaching job is happening.

## Common mistakes

- **Treating managers as approvers.** A manager who signed off on the program but never uses it signals that it is optional.
- **Adding a manager dashboard.** Managers do not need another login. Send the list to where they already work.
- **Asking managers to coach everything.** One skill per wave, or nothing changes.
- **Blaming the tool first.** Check whether managers ask about practice before you switch vendors. It is cheaper.

## What are the limits of manager reinforcement?

Managers cannot fix a weak program, a wrong skill choice or a team with too many reps per manager. Habel and colleagues' finding on span of control is a warning: a manager with 15 reps has less time per rep than one with 8. And the research here is mostly correlational, apart from the quasi-experiment in the 2025 working paper, so treat effect sizes as directional.

If you want to see how many manager and enablement hours your training plan really needs, book a free [20-minute Capacity Check](/#capacity-check).

## FAQ

### Why does sales training not stick?

Usually because nothing after the session asks reps to use it. Reps watch their manager. If the manager never mentions the program, never asks for a practice score and never coaches it on a live deal, reps conclude it does not matter.

### What is the sales manager's role in sales training?

The manager is the reinforcement layer. Enablement builds and runs the program; the manager endorses it, sets the focus, coaches it on real deals, asks about practice, reads the team's numbers and escalates reps who are stuck.

### How do you get busy sales managers to reinforce training?

Make each job take minutes and live inside meetings they already run. Give them a named list, one question to ask and a draft coaching note per rep. Have their own leader ask about it in the same way.

### How much time should managers spend on reinforcement?

Our estimate is 60 to 90 minutes a week for a manager with about ten reps, if enablement prepares the lists, scores and draft notes. Without that preparation, the same work can take three to four hours, and it does not happen.

### Does manager quality affect AI roleplay results?

A 2025 working paper by Habel, Ahearne and colleagues studied almost 2,000 salespeople and found an average performance gain of about 2% from AI roleplay training. Gains were larger when supervisors were high performers or had a narrow span of control.

### What is the difference between manager reinforcement and coaching?

Coaching is one of the six reinforcement jobs. Reinforcement also includes endorsing the program, setting one focus skill, asking about practice, reading the numbers and escalating. A manager can coach well and still let a program die by never mentioning it.

## Sources

- [SSRN: Habel, Ahearne, Tirunillai and Vandaveer Novak, Do AI role plays improve salesperson performance? Evidence from a longitudinal field study (2025)](https://ssrn.com/abstract=5717822)
- [Journal of Management: Blume, Ford, Baldwin and Huang, Transfer of Training: A Meta-Analytic Review (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1177/0149206309352880)
- [Human Resource Management: Saks and Belcourt, An Investigation of Training Activities and Transfer of Training in Organizations (2006)](https://doi.org/10.1002/hrm.20135)

# Sales onboarding: a ramp plan that starts before day one

> A strong sales onboarding program starts before day one: access, territory, accounts and a draft 30-day plan are ready when the rep arrives. A 30/60/90 ramp then moves from certification to supervised calls to an owned pipeline. Track time to first qualified meeting and time to first deal, not module completion. Average AE ramp is now 6.2 months.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/sales-onboarding-program/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- Average account executive ramp time reached 6.2 months in the Bridge Group's 2026 report, the highest in the study's history.
- The first week of onboarding is decided before day one: access, territory, accounts and a draft plan should be ready when the rep arrives.
- The manager should confirm a drafted onboarding plan in about ten minutes, not build one from a blank page.
- Track time to first qualified meeting and time to first deal; module completion says little about ramp.
- With fewer junior roles to learn in, scored simulations are how new reps get the repetitions that volume used to provide.

Most sales onboarding programs start on day one with a laptop, a login list and a binder. The rep fills in forms about accounts the company already knows, and the manager is asked to build a plan from scratch in a busy week. The result is a slow first month and a long ramp. This guide shows what to set up before day one, gives a 30/60/90 ramp plan, and defines the metrics that show whether onboarding works.

## Why does sales onboarding take so long?

Sales ramp is getting longer, mostly because deals are more complex. The Bridge Group's 2026 report on account executive models, based on 158 B2B companies, put average ramp at 6.2 months, the highest in the study's history. The report links the rise to deal complexity and larger buying committees, especially at higher deal sizes, and notes that companies are asking for more prior experience as ramp costs rise.

Onboarding quality is also low in general. Gallup found that only 12% of US employees say their company does a good job of onboarding, and only 29% of new hires feel fully prepared and supported to excel after onboarding. The same Gallup research found that employees were 3.4 times as likely to feel their onboarding was successful when their manager took an active role.

Both findings point to one lever: the manager, equipped early. See the [glossary entry for ramp time](/glossary/#ramp-time).

## What should be set up before a new sales rep's first day?

Everything the company already knows should be ready before the rep arrives. Onboarding still asks the rep for data the company holds. Read what exists instead, draft a plan, and let the manager edit it.

**Pre-start checklist (complete by day -3):**

1. **Access.** CRM, email, calendar, call recording, content platform, roleplay tool and LMS accounts work, and the rep is in the right Slack or Teams channels.
2. **Territory.** The account list, open opportunities, stages and last touches are pulled from the CRM into one view.
3. **The rep's baseline.** Prior industry, prior roles and a scheduled baseline skill assessment in week one.
4. **A draft 30-day plan.** Which accounts to research first, which skill to practice first, which calls to shadow.
5. **Roleplays from real accounts.** Two or three practice scenarios built from the rep's own territory, not generic personas.
6. **A buddy.** A named peer for daily questions in the first two weeks.
7. **Manager time.** Thirty minutes a day blocked in week one, and two coaching slots a week for the first month.

The manager's job is to confirm, not build. Ten minutes to review and edit a draft plan is realistic; building one from a blank page gets postponed. AI tools can draft much of this from CRM data. The limit: a messy CRM produces a confident, wrong plan, so the manager's review matters.

## The 30/60/90-day sales onboarding ramp plan

The plan moves the rep from learning to supervised selling to owning a pipeline. Adjust the milestones to your sales cycle; these fit a mid-market account executive with a cycle of about 60 to 90 days.

| Phase | Focus | Milestones | Evidence | Manager's job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Days -14 to 0 | Pre-start | Checklist complete, draft plan approved | Plan confirmed by manager | Review and edit the draft plan |
| Days 1–30 | Learn and certify | Buyer problems, product and sales motion learned. 10 calls shadowed. 5 scored roleplays from own accounts. Certification passed at 70 or above. First meetings booked. | Certification score, roleplay scores, meetings booked | Daily check-in in week one, two coaching sessions a week |
| Days 31–60 | Supervised selling | Rep leads discovery calls with manager present. First opportunities created. Pipeline built to an agreed target. | Calls led, manager call notes, opportunities created | Joins or reviews two calls a week, coaches one behavior |
| Days 61–90 | Own the pipeline | Rep runs full cycles alone. Deals advance past discovery. First win or a late-stage opportunity. | Stage progression, first deal or late-stage deal | One live-deal coaching session a week |
| Day 91 to full ramp | Build to quota | Monthly attainment climbs toward full quota | Attainment by month against the ramp curve | Normal coaching rhythm, tracked in coaching coverage |

### What to certify in the first 30 days

Test situations, not knowledge. A quiz about product features belongs in the LMS. The certification should ask the rep to handle a realistic moment with a scored buyer. One moment matters most for new reps: the opening of the second call. New reps often run good discovery, then open call two with a product demo, and everything learned in call one disappears. Certify that they can start call two by saying the buyer's problem back, asking what they got wrong and putting a number on it. See [problem-first selling](/guides/problem-first-selling/).

## Which sales onboarding metrics should you track?

Track the time it takes a rep to do real selling things, not how many modules they complete.

| Metric | Formula | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Time to first qualified meeting | Days from start date to the first meeting that meets your qualification rule | The earliest sign the rep can open conversations |
| Time to first opportunity | Days from start date to first opportunity created and accepted | Shows pipeline building has begun |
| Time to first deal | Days from start date to close of the first won deal the rep owned | Shows the rep can run a full cycle |
| Ramp time | Months from start date to the first month at or above full quota | The headline measure of onboarding |
| Certification score | Score on the 30-day certification, 0 to 100 | Early predictor to compare cohorts |

Report these by hiring cohort. A cohort that starts in January and one that starts in June face different pipelines, so compare each against its own baseline. See the [glossary entry for time to first deal](/glossary/#time-to-first-deal).

## Where do new reps learn judgment now?

New reps used to learn judgment through volume. Illustrative numbers for one junior rep's week: 200 dials built pattern recognition, 40 real conversations brought first objections, 10 genuine pushbacks gave practice in judgment, 2 recoveries were worth coaching and 1 lesson stuck. Now AI handles more of the dials and first conversations, and junior roles are scarcer.

The broader labor data shows the same direction. Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen at the Stanford Digital Economy Lab report that employment of 22–25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations now stands 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers (August 2026 revision), mainly through reduced hiring. The paper does not single out sales, so treat it as context, not a sales statistic.

The implication for onboarding: if real situations are scarcer, simulated situations with a score are how you refill the practice on purpose. Scored [AI roleplay](/guides/ai-roleplay-sales-training/) built from the rep's own accounts is the most direct way. The limit: a simulated objection is not a lost deal. The sting that makes a lesson stick is weaker. Simulation shortens the path; it does not replace real calls.

## Example: what one month of faster ramp is worth

Example: a company hires 40 account executives a year. Each carries an annual quota of $1.2 million, or $100,000 a month at full ramp. Average ramp is 6 months.

If a pre-start checklist and a 30/60/90 plan cut ramp by one month, each new rep reaches full productivity a month earlier. That adds about $100,000 of quota capacity per rep, or 40 × $100,000 = $4 million of capacity a year. Capacity is not revenue: apply your win rate and attainment to estimate the revenue effect. If the team attains 70% of quota on average, that is roughly $2.8 million of additional bookings potential, before any change in retention.

The cost side is mostly hours: about 6 enablement hours per new hire to prepare the pre-start pack, and about 8 manager hours in the first month. For 40 hires, that is 240 enablement hours a year.

## Common mistakes

- **Starting on day one.** Access problems and blank plans waste the first week.
- **Measuring completion.** Finishing 40 modules says nothing about whether the rep can run call two.
- **Generic roleplays.** Practice built from fictional companies feels like school. Build it from the rep's own accounts.
- **Leaving the manager out.** Gallup's 3.4 times finding is about the manager, not the content.
- **One ramp target for every role.** SDRs, mid-market AEs and enterprise AEs ramp at different speeds. Set targets by role.

## What are the limits of this ramp plan?

A ramp plan cannot fix a bad territory, an unclear ideal customer profile or a broken lead flow. It also depends on CRM data quality for the pre-start pack. Ramp benchmarks vary widely by deal size and segment, so treat the Bridge Group's 6.2 months as context and set your own baseline by role. And onboarding takes enablement hours: if you are hiring faster than your team can prepare, check your [enablement team size](/guides/sales-enablement-team-size/) against the plan, and read [why training fades without managers](/guides/sales-manager-reinforcement/).

If you want to know whether your team has the hours to run onboarding this way, a free [20-minute Capacity Check](/#capacity-check) gives you the estimate.

## FAQ

### How long does it take to ramp a new sales rep?

The Bridge Group's 2026 report puts average account executive ramp at 6.2 months across 158 B2B companies, the highest in the study's history. SDR and inside sales roles usually ramp faster; enterprise roles slower. Measure your own ramp by cohort.

### What is time to first deal?

It is the number of days from a rep's start date to the close of their first won deal that they sourced or owned. It is a leading signal of ramp because it shows a rep can run a full cycle, even before they reach full quota.

### What should be ready before a new sales rep starts?

Tool access, a territory and account list, a draft 30-day plan, a scheduled baseline skill assessment, roleplays built from the rep's real accounts, a named buddy and blocked time in the manager's calendar for the first two weeks.

### What should a 30/60/90 day sales onboarding plan include?

Days 1–30: learn the buyer, the product and the sales motion, and pass certification. Days 31–60: run calls with the manager present and build pipeline. Days 61–90: own a pipeline, advance deals and aim for the first win or a late-stage opportunity.

### How do you reduce sales ramp time?

Start before day one, test situations rather than knowledge, build practice from the rep's real accounts, and make the manager an active part of onboarding. Gallup found employees are 3.4 times as likely to rate onboarding successful when managers take an active role.

### Should new sales hires shadow experienced reps?

Yes, but with a purpose. Give them a short list of moments to watch for on each shadowed call, such as how the rep opens call two, then have them practice that moment in a scored roleplay the same week.

## Sources

- [The Bridge Group: 2026 AE Models, Motions and Metrics](https://www.bridgegroupinc.com/research/2026-ae-models-motions-metrics)
- [Gallup: 8 Practical Tips for Leaders for a Better Onboarding Process (2021)](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/353096/real-value-onboarding.aspx)
- [Stanford Digital Economy Lab: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen, Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/publications/canaries-in-the-coal-mine)

# How to build a sales skills scorecard reps and CROs both use

> Build a sales skills scorecard in five layers: activity at the base, then evidence from real calls, then a 0–100 score per skill that the rep can see, then a benchmark line at 70 drawn by cohort, then a link to quota. Score each skill from observable behaviors, credit the speaker who did the work, and calibrate managers every quarter.

Source: https://enablement.works/guides/sales-skills-scorecard/ · Updated 2026-11-06 · Enablement Works

## Key takeaways

- A 0–100 score per skill with a benchmark line at 70 is easier for reps, managers and CROs to act on than adjective bands like Developing or Strong.
- Score each skill from three to five observable behaviors, and show no score until there are at least three scored instances.
- Draw the benchmark by cohort, because an organization-wide average hides the team that is struggling.
- Score per speaker, not per call, or team selling will inflate the rep's scorecard.
- Skills that come up less than once a week should be scored in roleplays first, not waited for on live calls.

A sales skills scorecard is only useful if two very different readers use it. The rep needs to know what to do on the next call. The CRO needs to know which teams are short of which skills, and whether closing the gap moves quota. Most scorecards serve neither, because they use adjective bands that nobody can tell apart. This guide shows how to build one that serves both.

## What is a sales skills scorecard?

A sales skills scorecard is a regular record of how well each rep performs a small set of defined selling skills, based on evidence from real calls and scored practice. It is not a list of completed courses. It is the behavior level of the [four levels of evidence](/guides/sales-enablement-metrics/), made visible per rep and per team. The [glossary](/glossary/#skills-scorecard) has the short definition.

## Why does a 0–100 score work better than rating bands?

A number works better because people can compare it, trend it and try to beat it. Most assessments start with descriptive bands such as Developing, Consistent, Strong and Standout. In practice the same feedback comes back again and again: reps do not know what "Developing" means for them, managers cannot compare two people, and leaders cannot see a trend.

A score from 0 to 100 per skill fixes all three. Add a single index across skills for the overview, and draw a benchmark line at 70. Reps see their own numbers. The line gives them something to beat.

The concession: a number invites gaming. That is why call evidence sits underneath it. Faking a behavior across ten real calls is much harder than passing a quiz.

## What are the five layers of a scorecard?

Build the scorecard from the bottom up. Each layer depends on the one below it.

| Layer | What it shows | Who reads it most |
|---|---|---|
| 5. Quota link | Skill score against attainment, by cohort | CRO, sales leadership |
| 4. Benchmark by cohort | Share of each team at or above 70 | CRO, second-line managers |
| 3. Score per skill | 0–100 for each skill, visible to the rep | Rep, frontline manager |
| 2. Call evidence | Which behaviors showed up in which real conversations | Rep, frontline manager |
| 1. Raw activity | Completions and practice attempts | Enablement |

Raw activity is necessary but never sufficient. The quota link at the top is what makes the CRO keep reading.

## How do you score a skill from 0 to 100?

Define each skill as three to five observable behaviors, rate each behavior on each call or roleplay, and convert the total to a percentage. Observable means two people listening to the same call would agree whether it happened.

Rate each behavior 0 (absent), 1 (partly done) or 2 (done fully). Then:

**Skill score = points earned ÷ points possible × 100, averaged over the rep's last 10 scored instances.**

Show no score until a rep has at least three scored instances. One call is a hint, not a measure.

Example: the skill "get the buyer to name the cost of the problem" has four behaviors:

1. Asks the buyer to estimate the cost in their own numbers.
2. Plays the number back and confirms it.
3. Ties the number to a date or event.
4. Puts the number in the follow-up email.

A call that earns 2, 2, 1 and 1 scores 6 of 8 points, or 75. Across the last five instances the rep scored 75, 50, 63, 88 and 75, so the skill score is 70. With a four-behavior rubric, the benchmark of 70 means roughly six of eight points: most behaviors done fully, none ignored.

The line at 70 is our working benchmark, not a law. After two quarters, check where your top-attaining reps sit and move the line if the evidence says so.

## Where should the evidence come from?

Evidence should come from wherever the behavior happens: live calls for frequent skills, scored roleplays for rare ones, and email or documents for behaviors that never reach a recording.

### Count the moments before you rely on live calls

Some skills do not appear on enough calls to measure or learn live. Example arithmetic: a rep has about 5 customer calls a week, so 30 calls in a six-week cycle. If the moment for a skill appears in 1 call in 10, the rep gets 3 real chances in six weeks. Three attempts are not practice; they are three exams.

Our rule: if a skill comes up less than once a week, score it in a roleplay or simulator first and use live calls to coach the moments that do happen. Your own call data will give the real frequency per skill, and it varies a lot. [AI roleplay](/guides/ai-roleplay-sales-training/) makes the practice layer cheap enough to run weekly.

### Score per speaker, not per call

Call scores usually attach to the call, and the call belongs to the rep. When a manager or specialist joins and asks the best discovery questions, the rep's scorecard gets the credit. The rep may have spoken less than a fifth of the words. Their score rises while the gap stays put, and nobody finds out until their next solo call.

Credit each behavior to whoever demonstrated it, and show talk share by person. Fix speaker labels first; mislabeled speakers turn a per-speaker score into a new kind of noise.

### Include evidence that never reaches a recording

A call-only scorecard rates by silence: no evidence of a problem reads as no problem. Several deal-losing behaviors live elsewhere. Was the proposal walked through live or only emailed? Were concessions traded or given? Did the follow-up end with a dated ask? Is the buyer's own number in the business case? Start with three such behaviors and a human reviewer.

## How do you keep managers' scores consistent?

Calibrate every quarter. Ask all managers to score the same five calls with the rubric, then compare. A biostatistics guide to interrater reliability notes that many texts treat 80% agreement as the minimum acceptable, and suggests that a kappa below 0.60 indicates inadequate agreement ([McHugh, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3900052/)). Below 80% agreement on a behavior, rewrite that behavior's definition before you blame the managers.

Keep self-ratings out of the score. A meta-analysis of training transfer found that relationships were consistently inflated when the same source rated transfer in the same context ([Blume et al., 2010](https://doi.org/10.1177/0149206309352880)). A rep scoring their own call, or a manager scoring only the reps they coach, is that kind of source. Mix in scores from the AI rubric or a second reviewer.

## Example: the cohort view a CRO reads

Example: one skill, four teams, end of quarter.

| Cohort | Reps | Median score | Share at or above 70 | Change vs last quarter |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Team A | 25 | 74 | 64% | +12 points |
| Team B | 30 | 58 | 30% | +2 points |
| Team C | 20 | 71 | 55% | +9 points |
| Team D | 25 | 69 | 48% | +6 points |
| All reps | 100 | 67 | 49% | +7 points |

The organization median of 67 looks close to the line. The cohort view shows the real story: Team B has barely moved. That is where coaching time should go next quarter, and it is invisible in the org-wide average.

The quota link is the top layer. Example: reps at or above 70 reached 91% of quota on average, and reps below 70 reached 78%. Treat that as a correlation. Tenure and territory also drive both numbers, so compare reps of similar tenure before you claim a link. Kirkpatrick Partners makes a related point: the results that matter should be agreed with stakeholders in advance, not found afterward ([Kirkpatrick Partners](https://www.kirkpatrickpartners.com/the-kirkpatrick-model/)).

## Who sees what?

| Reader | What they see | What they do with it |
|---|---|---|
| Rep | Own scores, the line at 70, evidence clips | Picks one behavior for the next call |
| Frontline manager | Team scores, each rep's weakest skill | Runs one coaching conversation per rep per month |
| CRO | Cohort share at benchmark, trend, quota link | Moves coaching and program time to the weakest cohort |

The manager row connects directly to [coaching coverage](/guides/sales-coaching-coverage/). The CRO row belongs on the [monthly enablement report](/guides/enablement-report-for-cro/).

## Common mistakes

- **Using bands nobody can tell apart.** Use a number and one line.
- **Scoring too many skills.** Four to six at a time; ten spreads coaching too thin.
- **Crediting the call, not the speaker.** Team selling then inflates every rep's score.
- **Publishing individual rankings.** Show cohorts to leaders and own scores to reps.
- **Using scores as a promotion verdict.** They are an input to coaching. Once pay depends on them, the evidence gets worse.

The limit: a scorecard measures behaviors you can observe. Judgment that happens before any call, such as account research and prospecting choices, mostly stays invisible. Keep managers' judgment in the loop.

If you want help sizing the work of building and running a scorecard like this, the free 20-minute [Capacity Check](/#capacity-check) is a good first step.

## FAQ

### What should a sales skills scorecard include?

Four to six skills that matter for the current plan, each defined by three to five observable behaviors, scored 0 to 100. Add a benchmark line, a cohort view for managers and leaders, links to the call or roleplay evidence behind each score, and a quarterly view of score against attainment.

### Should sales reps see their own skill scores?

Yes. A score the rep cannot see becomes a judgment made about them, not a tool for them. Show each rep their own scores, the benchmark line and the evidence clips. Do not publish rankings of individual reps.

### Why use a number instead of rating bands?

Bands like Developing, Consistent and Strong are hard to tell apart, hard to compare across people and hard to trend. A number shows movement, a benchmark line gives the rep something to beat, and leaders can average it by cohort.

### How many skills should a sales scorecard track?

Four to six at a time. More than that spreads coaching too thin and makes every score noisier. Retire a skill from active coaching once most of the cohort sits above the benchmark for two quarters.

### Can AI score sales calls accurately?

AI can score observable behaviors on calls reasonably well when the rubric is specific and speakers are labeled correctly. Check it the same way you check managers: score a sample of calls by hand and compare. Treat any score from a single call as a hint, not a verdict.

### Should skill scores be used in performance reviews?

Use them as an input to coaching, not as a promotion or compensation verdict. Once scores decide pay, reps start optimizing the score instead of the skill, and the evidence gets worse.

## Sources

- [McHugh, Interrater reliability: the kappa statistic, Biochemia Medica (2012)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3900052/)
- [Blume, Ford, Baldwin and Huang, Transfer of training: a meta-analytic review, Journal of Management (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1177/0149206309352880)
- [Kirkpatrick Partners: The Kirkpatrick Model](https://www.kirkpatrickpartners.com/the-kirkpatrick-model/)
